# Status

Where the project is, what is settled, and what comes next. Updated 2026-08-13.

The detailed evidence for everything asserted here is in [`notes.md`](notes.md),
which is a working log rather than a summary — every claim below traces to a
measurement recorded there. The format is specified in
[`sidecar.md`](sidecar.md).

## Where it stands

**The server has accounts.** Spec A2 shipped on 2026-08-18, and **four
whole-branch reviews of it found fifteen things each** — a rate limit the spec
required on the `Authorization: Basic` path that had never been written, a claim
route that would take an empty password for the server's only administrator, an
enumeration test whose floor sat six routes below what shipped while reading
nothing at all of the exemption list it was credited with policing, and, in the
fourth round, a claim route open on a library its owner had already set up.
Every one is fixed on the branch; `notes.md` has the reproductions.

**The rate did not fall across the four rounds, and that is the finding about
the process rather than about the code.** Roughly a quarter of each round came
from the round before it — the clearest being the decoy hash added in round two
to close a timing oracle, which turned a documented and until-then-harmless
rate-limiter gap into an unauthenticated denial of service that round four
found. The rest was new ground each time, and the findings got deeper rather
than repeating: round one was structural (missing guards, wrong status codes),
round four semantic (two functions disagreeing about what "claimed" means).
Fifteen is what a round *reports*, not what exists. Nothing tracks which
invariants have been checked — coverage measures which lines ran — so each
reviewer re-samples the whole branch. A fifth round was not commissioned for
that reason; mutation testing is what measures whether a test can see a defect,
and it is the next thing on this branch's list rather than another reader.

What shipped: every `/api` and
`/opds` route resolves to a `Principal` before it runs, from a session cookie or
from `Authorization: Basic` — a password for a browser, a `tyk_`-prefixed API key
for an OPDS client, and the prefix is what keeps a 400-page volume from paying
argon2 four hundred times. Passwords hash with argon2id; session tokens and API
keys are 256-bit CSPRNG secrets stored as sha256 and never held raw. The two
hardcoded `LOCAL_USER = 1` constants are gone, so two readers of one work hold
two positions and two sets of notes, which the database could always express and
the server could not. `taiyaku library user` and `library key` administer it, and
promotion reaches the row spec A seeded rather than inserting beside it —
inserting would have orphaned every note recorded since, silently. What it
deliberately does not do is in §11 of its design; what it left open is O54
*(O54 has since closed — see its entry above)*, O55 *(also since closed, by
spec C2's second half: Panels does accept a `tyk_` key)* and O57 *(since
closed too, on 2026-10-12 — see its entry above)*.

**L0 works.** The aligner reads two editions, pairs their pages, and writes a
sidecar. It has been measured against eleven series and holds up on every case the
design anticipated, plus several it did not.

**`taiyaku serve` with no paths serves the whole library.** Spec C1 §5.3: the reader is handed sidecar paths on argv and a scanned work has none, so a browse UI over a derived library was a grid of covers that opened nothing. `works::from_library` projects every row instead, and a work with no `sidecar_path` is served from rows and corrected into rows — `patch_alignments` writes the file first *and only when there is one*, which for a scanned work means the correction's only copy is in the database until somebody runs `library export`. That cost is stated rather than solved; minting a `taiyaku.json` would have made the server a writer into a tree spec B never opens for writing.

**The reader now has a front end.** Milestones 1 through 3 shipped: page
reading is a crate of its own, `taiyaku serve` hands an HTTP client the
sidecar, any page by index, and where you were, and it can now read those pages
from a Stump instance as well as local disk and publish an OPDS feed grouping a
work's editions. M5a shipped the browser reader that draws it: single-page,
two-page spread and continuous-scroll modes, a swap between editions that
never writes position, a gap state that names an unpaired slot rather than
silently landing near it — *no longer the default since `gap-fallback`, marked
here rather than rewritten: another edition's page is drawn there and that gap
is one press of its mark away, per the "Fall back to another edition…" entry
below* — and a floating chrome — filmstrip and slot readout — that never
reflows the page underneath. M5d shipped the correction UI: a reader can point
at the right counterpart in the filmstrip and have the fix
written into the sidecar as `by: "hand"`, surviving a re-solve. `verify`'s
contact sheet remains read-only, but it is no longer the only way to see or
change what the aligner decided. A defect M5a had carried since it shipped
closed just after: an arrow steps by what is *drawn* — a group — rather than
by slot, so crossing a joined spread no longer takes two presses and a swap
always answers from the half a reader can see. **M5c shipped annotations, and
with them the one thing no other reader can offer: a note written on the raw
is readable while reading the English**, resolved through the same call the
swap makes, marked in the margin, and listed — including the notes that cannot
be reached from where the reader is standing, which are marked rather than
hidden.

**L1 shipped zoom, and with it the first thing the alignment does for a reader
that a side-by-side viewer cannot do at all.** A reader zoomed into a speech
balloon on the raw presses the swap and lands on the same balloon in English:
the rect they are looking at is mapped onto the other edition's page and the
viewport fitted around the result. A page turn carries the view and re-clamps;
continuous scroll is untouched and keeps fit-whole. **Which transform does the
mapping was measured rather than argued, and the measurement went against the
design**: of the two candidates it named, one turned out worse than doing
nothing, and what ships is a third neither had proposed. §5 below is the record.
Nothing in the sidecar, the aligner or the server changed to make it work.

**Three reader complaints landed on top of it, and the browser corrected two
designs on the way.** Pages fill their box now, the two halves of a spread meet
at the seam, and `?` or `h` lists every key the reader answers — generated from
the same table `intentOf` dispatches from, so there is no second copy to drift.
§6 below is the record, and the parts worth reading are the two failures: the
seam's design closed the gap on the wrong element and a measurement said so, and
closing it introduced a regression that put every annotation marker 376px from
its artwork until the same pass caught that too.

**Two more came from reading in two-page mode, and both were rules that were
right about one page and had never been asked about two.** A pair's halves each
appeared as its own decode settled — measured at a median 89.7 ms apart, every
turn tearing — and they now present together through one barrier. And the two
editions on either side of a swap drew pairs one page out of phase, because
pairing was anchored at slot 0 of each edition independently. **Pair boundaries
are now a property of the work rather than of an edition**: wherever any edition
joins a spread, that boundary is mapped into the hub's slot space, unioned with
every other edition's, and every edition — the hub included — takes its pairing
from the one grouping that results. Swaps that keep the pair intact go from 206
of 580 to 581 of 590. §8 below is the record, and it has two parts worth
reading. What the defect was *not*: the obvious diagnosis was an alignment
error, and a shift test over 12 alignments in 9 volumes says the aligner has
none — after the scan itself was corrected for the one-to-one constraint that
had made four volume tails look broken. And what the first fix missed: deriving
only the *spokes* from the hub scored 96% and left the hub unable to follow a
boundary only a spoke has, which a reader found at one press.

**It can be deployed.** `taiyaku serve --web DIR` serves the built web app
beside the API, so one process and one port serve both; a path no route
matched is the app's, except under `/api` and `/opds`, which keep their 404.
The repository builds an image (`Dockerfile`), CI pushes it to the forge's
registry on every merge to `main` whose pipeline passes, after running it,
and `README.md`'s "Running it on a server" is how it is meant to run on the
NAS. Spec
`2026-10-04-day-to-day-deployment-design.md`, Part B.

**The store keeps libraries.** A library is a name and one or more directories
(migration 15; migration 16 strips a name of all surrounding white space and makes names unique regardless of case), and a grant names a library rather than a directory. A
directory may be in several libraries: one directory, with one set of settings
and one scan, linked to each (migration 19). One
derive runs over the whole store, and proposals pair series wherever their
files are: a library decides what an account sees and what a library page
lists, and not what a work or a series is (migration 18). A byte-identical
volume in two libraries is one work, one member held under both directories;
two different files of one volume under one edition key are one edition, one
page sequence through both, in two libraries as in one. **Such an edition is
narrowed** for an account granted some of those libraries and not all: it is
shown the files its libraries show, its pages numbered 1 to n, while its
positions and notes are kept in the full numbering — the reader sends each
one's page with it, so a write read before a renumbering lands on its page
(O240) — and it cannot write that edition's ground truth or correct its
alignments (spec §3.8, O239). Only an
administrator, by a browser session or the account's password, never a key,
writes either document, and a key still reads both (O58).
Configuration → Split editions lists each such edition for administrators,
with what each library sees of it. A store `main`
made opens, migrates and rescans that way on a copy of the test library
(`notes.md`, "Overlapping libraries PR 1 on the test library"), a merged
edition is narrowed on it (`notes.md`, "Narrowing a merged edition on the test
library"), and a build after the branch's fixes did both again and removed a
copy's directory (`notes.md`, "PR 1 after its fixes, on the test library").
`taiyaku library
libraries` lists them, `library scan --add PATH --library NAME` files a directory
under one, linking it where another library holds it, and `library user
grant-library` grants one. Configuration →
Libraries makes, renames, scans and removes them, and moves a directory between
them (Parts F2a and F2b). Adding a directory another library holds links it,
and it keeps the settings it has there; a directory several libraries hold
says so on its page, which offers Remove from this library, deleting nothing,
beside Remove this directory, from every library. Removing a library leaves
each of its directories another library holds to the libraries that still hold
it.
A library can be removed, and its last directory removed, moved away or taken
out of it, even
where it is some account's only grant; that account then sees no library
until an administrator grants one, and `library user every-library` lifts a
limit (O220).
Every account's sidebar lists the libraries it is granted, each with a page of
its own that narrows the grid and the continue strip; search narrows to one;
and OPDS lists them twice, by the directories each shows and by work, each
work with a member under them listed with every edition the grant allows
(Part F3). A library shows its own directories and each directory nested in
one of them that its walk would reach, and the walk of a directory skips each
directory nested in it, so a file is scanned under the deepest directory that
holds it, by that directory's rules. Specs `2026-10-05-libraries-design.md`
and, for libraries whose directories overlap,
`2026-11-02-overlapping-libraries-design.md` (its PRs 1, 2 and 3).

## What is built

Six crates, 4587 tests, plus 5,766 in `web/`'s TypeScript — 2,006 in the `node`
project and 3,760 in the `jsdom` one — and two thousand four hundred and
nineteen more in a **browser** project of its own, no dependencies beyond
`image`, `zip`, `sha2`, `rayon`, `base64` and `serde`, and `compress-tools` in `taiyaku-read` behind its optional `rar-libarchive` feature, linking the system libarchive and taken from the owner's fork by commit (O382), with `pkg-config` at build time for libarchive's version, plus `axum`, `tokio`,
`tower`, `tower-http` (feature `fs`, for `--web`), `ureq` and `jxl-oxide` (since O130, for JPEG XL pages) in the server, `tikv-jemallocator` in `taiyaku-cli` (since O349, the `taiyaku` binary's allocator, with its `background_threads` feature; jemalloc's C is built by `tikv-jemalloc-sys` with jemalloc's own `configure` and `make`), `rusqlite` (features `["backup", "bundled", "functions"]`,
compiling SQLite into the binary since O265, because no stable Debian release
ships the SQLite that fixes RUSTSEC-2026-0459; the system libsqlite3 had been
chosen on build time, measured at 1 m 43 s to build bundled against 3.06 s on a
32-core machine, against a CI with no cargo cache and a ten-minute job budget)
in the new `taiyaku-library` crate, which
`taiyaku-serve` also names directly for the slug-to-row bridge, `argon2` for
spec A2's password hashing — the one genuinely new crate on that branch,
measured at 1.70 CPU-seconds for it and its five transitive dependencies
against 138.85 for a clean workspace build, with no inference drawn about CI's
budget — and `regex` in
the same crate for the scanner's rule layer's `regex`-kind rules (§4) — and
`zip` in it too since spec C3 §6's ComicInfo write-back, already in the tree
through `taiyaku-read` and named directly because this crate's own code now
rewrites an archive rather than only reading one — no
backtracking, so a pattern typed into C4's text box cannot produce
catastrophic behaviour, and already in `Cargo.lock` at 1.13.1 pulled in
transitively, so naming it here adds a dependency edge rather than a new
crate to build — and `ignore` in it since O92's scanner half, for applying
`root.exclude_globs` to the walk: 0.4.33, and **three new crates rather than
the ten `cargo add` suggests** — `ignore`, `globset` and `bstr` — measured
against this workspace's lock on 2026-09-09, since `notify` already supplies
`walkdir`, `same-file`, the `crossbeam-*` trio and `winapi-util`; `globset`
alone would have cost two of the same three and cannot express negation, and
a hand-rolled matcher would have been the second, drifting reimplementation
`rules.rs` already argues against — and `notify` in the same crate again, for §8 of the scanner
spec's watch probe: 8.2.0, verified with `cargo add notify --dry-run` on
2026-08-17, and unlike `regex` this one is genuinely new rather than already
in `Cargo.lock`, bringing a small subtree with it. **Four crates on Linux**,
re-measured 2026-08-18 against the merge base: `notify`, `notify-types`,
`inotify` and `inotify-sys`. The rest of its subtree — `bitflags`, `libc`,
`log`, `mio`, `walkdir`, `same-file` — was in the lockfile already. Seven new
package *names* appear in `Cargo.lock` in total, the other three being
`fsevent-sys`, `kqueue` and `kqueue-sys`, which no Linux build compiles; the
Windows entries in that diff are second versions of crates already present,
not new names. This said "sixteen crates on Linux" and no reading of the
lockfile or of `cargo tree` gives sixteen. Measured rather than assumed: a clean
`cargo build --workspace --all-targets --all-features` on this same 32-core
machine cost about 6% more CPU time with it than without (262 against 248
CPU-seconds) — not run through CI itself, and a 32-core box parallelises a
build differently than the runner CI actually uses, so that is what was
measured and nothing is inferred from it about the ten-minute budget —
`wasm-bindgen` in the binding, `react`, `react-router` and `vite` in `web/` —
`react-router` (8.3.0) **the first runtime dependency beyond React since the
project began**, kept over a fifty-line hand-rolled router that spec C1 §13
had also weighed, a decision closed 2026-08-20 rather than left open, for
scroll restoration, nested routes and navigation blocking, all things this UI
wants and all things tedious to get right twice. Measured on `pnpm build`:
the shipped bundle moved from 294.37 kB raw / 94.54 kB gzip to 337.22 kB raw /
109.30 kB gzip, **+42.85 kB raw / +14.76 kB gzip**, of which `react-router`
alone cost +37.59 kB raw / +13.16 kB gzip measured in isolation when it landed
(Task 7), and `tract-onnx` as a dev-dependency of `taiyaku-cli` alone, for
phase 3's gated measurement — it reaches no binary and no other crate. The
style pass's first PR added `@fontsource/shippori-mincho-b1` and
`@fontsource/zen-kaku-gothic-new`, which are fonts and CSS rather than code.
In apparent bytes, the built `web/dist` held 604,783 before them, its CSS
asset 16,306 bytes, and 34,294,658 with them: a 713.98 kB CSS asset (312.31 kB
gzip), JS essentially unmoved — `main` 191.45 kB (58.04 kB gzip), `label`
10.87 kB (4.29 kB gzip), the shared chunk 215.92 kB (68.92 kB gzip) — and the
growth 570 `.woff2` font files totalling 14,841,516 bytes and 574 `.woff`
fallbacks totalling 18,148,448. The same PR then strips the `.woff` fallbacks
from the build, since every browser that can draw the tokens loads woff2:
`web/dist` now holds 16,005,973 bytes, with no `.woff` file and a 573.60 kB
CSS asset (243.22 kB gzip). The thirty-two run under Vitest's browser mode
over Playwright's
Chromium, and cover only what no Node environment can answer: `jsdom` has no
layout engine and no real `HTMLImageElement.decode()`, and every defect the page
area has shipped was one or the other. They are **not** a CI job — CI's `web`
job has no cache and would download a browser on every run — so `pnpm -C web run test:coverage`, which
is what CI and `check-all.sh` both run, stays the `node` and `jsdom` projects, and
`check-all.sh` runs the browser one separately and locally, naming it
unmeasured when the browser is absent. That adds `@vitest/browser`,
`@vitest/browser-playwright` and `playwright` to `web/`'s dev dependencies;
the runtime list above is unchanged. That list did not grow for L1: zoom is a CSS transform and
a page of arithmetic, and its corpus experiment fingerprints with `image` and
`rayon` exactly as `align` already did. Twenty-six of the 4587 are standing checks in
the corpus run (`corpus::`) — seventeen in `crates/taiyaku-cli` (ten in `src/corpus.rs`,
three in `src/corpus/tests.rs` and four in `src/score_corpus.rs`; the three in
`corpus/tests.rs` and two of `score_corpus.rs`'s, which run on fixtures, need
no corpus), five in
`crates/taiyaku-serve/src/corpus.rs`, two in
`crates/taiyaku-library/src/corpus.rs`, two in
`crates/taiyaku-read/src/corpus.rs` (this read "nineteen … ten … five"
until 2026-09-09, which was never arithmetic that worked and never named the
library's two; measured off the corpus run rather than recounted) — two of those added here, over spec C2's
own material: a real multi-member edition downloading as a readable zip, and a
real single-member edition served byte for byte — two in
`crates/taiyaku-cli/src/score_corpus.rs` and two in
`crates/taiyaku-library/src/corpus.rs` — the newest of those checking the
scanner itself, walk through derive, over the corpus's settled material
(whole-branch review's I9) — one of which also needs
`TAIYAKU_STUMP_URL` and `TAIYAKU_STUMP_KEY`; each skips cleanly when what it
needs is absent, so CI stays green without the corpus or a reachable Stump.
One measures composition
against a direct solve — 2,427 page comparisons, 0.91% loss, 0.00% disagreement.
One measures that the server and the aligner agree about what page N is — 617
pages across 3 editions, no disagreement. One measures that a note can be anchored to
every slot of every real edition — 629 anchors across three, two of which join
spreads and so have more slots than pages, which is the case a four-page
fixture cannot tell apart from a page check. One measures that the server and
Stump serve the same bytes for a member both hold — 187 pages compared byte-for-byte,
no disagreement, and 8 members this Stump instance does not hold recorded as
absent rather than silently skipped. Two pin credit-page classification against
both fan editions the corpus holds — Go-Toubun's four pages and Kaguya's single
known false positive, asserted as *sets* rather than counts, since four of six
is reachable by classifying the wrong four; see §4 below. The remaining six run
duplicate resolution over real duplicate sets and are listed in §2 below with
what each one measured. `check-all.sh` runs all twelve with `--nocapture`
against an absolute, canonicalised `TAIYAKU_CORPUS`, so a green gate shows what
each one measured, or says plainly that it did not run them at all. **It runs
them under `--release`**, and its `test` job runs with `TAIYAKU_CORPUS` removed
from the environment so they run once rather than twice — the whole gate is
about 15 seconds warm, against a run that was killed at 1h09m before that split.
The debug profile is the only one with overflow checks and `debug_assert!`, so
the unit tests are what exercise those and `--corpus-debug` puts the corpus
checks back under them; `docs/ci.md`, "Two profiles, and the gate that took an
hour", is the record.

**Nine further tests are gated on `TAIYAKU_CORPUS` and are deliberately not
among those twelve.** Seven are one-off measurements rather than checks, and
all seven are built the same way for the same reason: gated, skipping cleanly
when the variable is unset, calling the detector's own functions rather than
copies of them, and asserting only that they measured something — never a
quality figure, because a check that fails when the thing it measures improves
is not a measurement. **Three of the seven are phase 3's**, all in
`crates/taiyaku-cli/src/model_experiment.rs` and additionally gated on
`TAIYAKU_MODEL`: the head-to-head table against `detect_page`; — added
2026-08-12 — the measurement of whether the model groups a page's balloons the
same way on the raw and on the English edition, which is a pairing question
rather than a labelling one and reads no truth boxes at all; and, the same day,
a sweep of the model's confidence floor `BLK_CONF` over eight values, which is
`band_sweep.rs`'s shape applied to a constant taken verbatim from upstream and
never measured here. All three are described in the L2 entry below. This
sentence said "four" until the second landed, having missed the first one; the
count is not gate-checked, only the two totals above are. Two more are
described below; the remaining two are L2b's, and are
`crates/taiyaku-cli/src/truth_population.rs`, which measures what text is made
of from inside 478 hand-drawn truth boxes, and
`crates/taiyaku-cli/src/band_sweep.rs`, which scores the detector at eight
values of `BAND`'s `lo` over all 45 labelled pages and is what fixed it. Both
read their pages through `score::resolve_labelled`, so they measure exactly the
pages `taiyaku score` scores. `notes.md`, "What text is made of, measured
against 480 hand-drawn boxes" and "Where the band goes, measured at eight bands
over 478 hand-drawn boxes", are what each one printed. The band sweep is about
51 seconds under `--release`: it detects all eight bands inside one decode pass,
where re-entering the decode per band would be 360 full-resolution decodes to
score 45 pages. The other two measure the reader and the books, and this
paragraph said "seven" without them until 2026-11-17:
`crates/taiyaku-cli/src/borrow_frequency.rs`, how often a reader meets a gap
(`notes.md`, "How often a reader meets a gap, and who actually lends"), and
`crates/taiyaku-cli/src/book_experiment.rs`, how well two editions of a book
align, measured against keys.

The `match_experiment` tests gated on `TAIYAKU_MATCH_LIBRARY`, and `nas_timing`,
gated on `TAIYAKU_MATCH_NAS_ROOT` alone, are the content-matching measurement,
recorded in `notes.md`, "Edition matching by content: PR 1's measurement
(2026-11-16)".

`crates/taiyaku-cli/src/region_experiment.rs` is L2a's: why the text-block
detector fails, run against real pages. It prints, per sampled page, the
component count, the fraction of components under 5px, the scale each of three
candidate rules derives, the gap that follows, **how many blocks survive each of
the four filters in order**, the largest block `MAX_BLOCK_AREA` discarded, and
the axis flagged against the edition's true reading direction — and, since the
measurement below that asked what the one edition clearing the bar was actually
finding, **what every surviving block is made of**: its size, how many
components it holds, how many of those are under 5px against how many of the
page's are, and their median size, plus the page's own pixel dimensions, the
smear gap as a fraction of them, the largest component *before* any smearing,
and what each of the four filters rejected across the whole sample. It exists because
the first version of this diagnosis was a throwaway program, discarded once
`notes.md` was written — which left the survey's `regions:` lines reproducible
and the diagnosis behind them not. It calls `detect.rs`'s own functions rather
than copies of them, so nothing in it can drift from what `taiyaku regions`
does; the discarded program copied them and needed a cross-check against the
real command to show the copy was faithful. About seven seconds under
`--release`. See `notes.md`, "The text-block detector, measured against four
works, and why it does not work yet", "The scale rule, tried three ways, and
neither candidate clears the bar", and "The edition that clears the bar is the
one finding no text" — the last of which names the command that reprints every
figure in it.

`crates/taiyaku-cli/src/geometry_experiment.rs` is L1's one-off
measurement of which derived transform a swap should map through, and it stays a
measurement rather than becoming a check: it asserts only that it measured
something — a non-empty sample, a search that found a minimum in every volume,
every residual finite — so that a glob matching no volume cannot print an empty
table and pass, which is the one failure a measurement must not have.
`check-all.sh` reaches none of these four — its corpus job filters on
`corpus::`, and its `test` job now runs with `TAIYAKU_CORPUS` removed from the
environment — so the twelve above are still twelve. All four are excluded from
the per-file coverage floor by name, in the `--ignore-filename-regex` that
appears twice in `check-all.sh` and twice in `ci.yml`; a gated experiment that
skips in CI would otherwise report near-zero coverage and fail the floor. That second half is new:
until 2026-08-08 the `test` job inherited the variable and ran both of these in
**debug**, which is how a gate run came to be killed at 1h09m inside
`geometry_experiment` alone. This one also wants `--release`, under which it
takes about a minute against about forty without. Not promoting it was decided in
advance, by a rule fixed before the number existed (the L1 design's §4), and
the rule's first branch fired. It also could not have been promoted as written:
the transform it picked is TypeScript, so a Rust corpus check would re-measure
page dimensions no code in this repository can alter and go green while the
browser did something else. The unit tests beside `mapRect` are what guards
`mapRect`. See `notes.md`, "The exposure, and why there is no standing check".

`taiyaku-core` is the portable half — no I/O, so it compiles to WebAssembly:

| Module | Holds |
| ------ | ----- |
| `solve` | similarity, per-pair floor calibration, Needleman-Wunsch, run compression, confidence, verdict |
| `slot` | spread detection, slot expansion, reading direction |
| `sidecar` | the `taiyaku.json` format — parse, emit, judge, merge an edition in. `from_json` **refuses a document declaring a format version newer than this build reads**, so no command silently strips the fields it has no name for and writes the result back stamped version 1. The library's own import checked that at its two entry points and `align --write`, `credits --write` and `regions` did not; one check where every command parses is what makes the answer the same in all of them |
| `route` | which path a lookup walks between two editions, and the page it lands on |

Four of the other five touch the disk or the network. `taiyaku-wasm` touches
neither — it is portable like the core, and separate from it so the core's API
is not shaped by what can cross the JavaScript boundary.

| Crate | Holds |
| ----- | ----- |
| `taiyaku-read` | how a member becomes pages — archives, directories, natural order, page counts, content hashes, one page by index. It also holds what a *name* and what a container's *bytes* mean, both moved here on the scanner branch so `taiyaku-library` can call them without a second implementation: `volume_number` (marker or first digit run — `inventory`'s, since it is handed a directory that is a volume by construction), `volume_number_marked` and `chapter_number` (marker required, since a rule applies to every filename in a library), and `Format`/`sniff`, which answers what a container is from its first 512 bytes rather than its extension — `scan_entry.format` is sniffed, never derived from a suffix, because a zip named `.cbr` and a RAR named `.cbz` are both routine. It also reads an EPUB as text: `read_book` (`book`), phase 1 of the books work, turns one into an ordered list of blocks, parsing each document as strict XML and refusing one that does not parse by name. It reads RAR too, in a build with its `rar-libarchive` feature, through the private `rar` interface and its libarchive backend (`rar::Backend`, `rar::libarchive`); a build without the feature refuses a RAR by name, saying this build reads no RAR. A library's derive admits only what `Format::is_readable` admits, which takes in RAR in a build with the feature (`Format::PAGED`, since O391); a build without it counts a RAR as unreadable under `rar` |

A work's visibility under a grant is decided on `member.root_id` (migration 6), on the member rather than on the work because a work spans roots by design; an account that sees every library applies no filter at all, which is what stops the upgrade emptying every account's shelf. Since O220 that is the account's `every_library` setting (migration 17) rather than an empty grant, and an account limited to libraries and granted none sees nothing. **A hand-imported work has no series** — `import` never writes `series_id`, and cannot, since `taiyaku.json` has no field for it — so the grid and search both return `{ series, unfiled }`, without which every library predating spec B opened on an empty page. The schema also carries `collection`/`tag` (spec C1's browse UI, not built). The rest of what used to be listed beside them as unpopulated is spec B's scanner, and `derive.rs` is what populates it: the walk writes `scan_entry`/`dir_state` under a `root` and decides nothing about them, the rule engine maps a `rel_path` onto a series, an edition key, a volume and a chapter, and derivation turns those two into `series`, `series_title` (which is what the per-title FTS indexes, and what `librarydoc::find_series_by_title` looks a series up by, so a series row without one would be invisible to both), and — through `import::scanned`, so `work`/`edition`/`member` keep exactly one writer — the works themselves. `series_id` and `volume` on `work` are the two columns that import cannot write, because `taiyaku.json` has no field for either, so derivation sets them directly; they are also the pair the hub lookup reads back, since `content_key` cannot be computed until the hub is known and the hub must be fixed when the work is created. **A derive opens no file** except to hash a member nothing has hashed yet, and writes that digest back onto `scan_entry` — which is the whole of §2's claim: editing a rule re-derives the library with the tree deleted, and `derive/tests.rs` deletes it to prove there is no other route. Two rules keep that from doing damage. **A scan replaces editions and members and touches nothing else**: `import::scanned` leaves `alignment`, `run` and `page_flag` alone, because a walk cannot know how two editions correspond or which pages are a group's donation cards, and until 2026-08-17 it deleted all three from an empty document on every rescan — so a rescan after an `align --write` dropped hand-corrected runs, and a `library export` in the window wrote a sidecar with no alignments over the reader's own copy. *Since content matching's PR 3 a derive also writes `by = solver` alignments for pairs of volumes matched at the bar (`import::put_solver_alignment`), never where a person answers for the pair; `import::scanned` still leaves the rest alone.* The cost is stated rather than discovered: a rule edit that removes an edition an alignment names leaves that edge dangling, which `runs_of` reports and `quality_of` answers `None` to, so the work still projects and its hub still serves. **A directory is a member only if no ancestor of it is one**: the fact layer records a container and its children alike, so without that test a volume produced a member for itself *and* one per chapter. **The evidence for that used to be a citation of `docs/sidecar.md`'s "7 of 57 archives nesting pages in folders", and that document is measuring something else** — entry names *inside* a zip, which never become `scan_entry` rows at all and so cannot produce a member either way. The on-disk measurement that does support it, taken 2026-08-18 over `corpus/`: 121 directories hold page images directly, and 107 of them sit beneath another that also does — every one under `incoming/`, this corpus's untidied dump, which is exactly the shape a real library arrives in — its pages counted twice, its pieces made editions of nothing, and, where the chapters carry no volume marker, the volume they are plainly inside reported as needing an `attach-chapters` decision. **And only if nothing *inside* it is one either, unless a rule marked it a volume**: a container the rules gave no volume is a name in a path rather than something anybody released, so it stands aside for whatever holds the material — without that half, `Series/Extras/Art Book` counted five pages as ten and three levels gave three members, and taking the container instead (the first fix for it) turned 107 corpus members into 40, collapsing `incoming/bocchi`'s five editions into one 439-page sequence. A container the rules *did* mark as a volume still wins, which is the sentence above: `Series - v01/c001` is a piece of `v01`, not a work beside it. A **page-less** container wins nothing at all — a volume directory holding `.cbz` files takes `pages = Some(0)` from the walk, and it used to suppress the archive that held the pages and then hash to the digest of nothing, so every such directory collided on `content_key` and one row swallowed the rest. **Entries the rules gave neither a volume nor a chapter are keyed individually**, by `rel_path`: keyed on `(series, NULL)` they merged, so `ONE PIECE/001..004` — bare numbers, which `volume_number_marked` deliberately refuses — became one work of 18 concatenated pages, and a volume-less group is therefore addressed by its own member paths rather than by `(series_id, NULL)`, which no longer names one row. A scanned work with a volume also has a **stable address**, `(series_id, volume)`, probed after `content_key` exactly as a document-backed work's `sidecar_path` is: `content_key` hashes the hub edition's member digests, so adding a page, repacking an archive or fixing a scan moved it, the key lookup missed, and a second `work` row was inserted while the reader's progress, notes and history stayed on the first — measured on 2026-08-17, and triggered by the most ordinary events in this corpus. Content still decides first, so a volume whose bytes are unchanged follows them wherever it is renamed or renumbered to, and a duplicated download cannot turn one repeated file into a failed derive of a whole library. **What makes the address probe safe is that order and a counter, not any uniqueness of the address itself**: an address can be vacated and reoccupied — remove volume 1, renumber volume 2 into its place and repack it — and the probe then hands volume 1's row, and a reader's volume-1 position with it, to what was physically volume 2. Without the probe that same scan mints a third row and strands the position outright, so it is a trade made deliberately and `rekeyed` counts every time it fires. What that address probe reconciles is **counted** as `rekeyed`, and what the suppression drops is **counted** rather than dropped in silence: a rule set that accidentally made a series directory speak for its volumes would swallow every one of them, and a report with no number for that reads exactly like a library that happens to hold nothing — the same reason `check-all.sh` refuses to print a bare "all green" when something was skipped. **Any derivation outcome that changes what a person sees and cannot be inferred from the other counts gets a field**, which is the rule `suppressed` and `rekeyed` were built on and which `kept_editions`, `merged` and `unrecognised_kinds` follow too: `kept_editions`, editions standing on a work that this derive did not derive — a scan no longer deletes an edition it did not name, since "the scan never saw this" and "a rule edit removed it" are one statement from in there and a deleted hand-aligned edition is unrecoverable while an orphan is visible and fixable — `merged`, entries that joined an edition another entry had already opened, which is right for the chapters of a volume and wrong for anything else and which derivation cannot always tell apart, and `unrecognised_kinds`, editions whose rules named an `edition.kind` the column's closed set does not hold, so none was written. A scan is also barred from writing `work.title`, `work.reading`, `work.hub` and `edition.label` over a row that already has them: it derives a title from a filename and a direction from a constant, while a document carries what a person or the aligner established, and `import` + `scan` + `export --in-place` was measured rewriting a reader's own `taiyaku.json` from "Go-Toubun no Hanayome, volume 1" / ltr / "Japanese raw" to "Series - v01" / rtl / "raw". The cost, since nothing records whether a title came from a person or from an earlier derive: a work this scanner minted keeps the title it first derived, so a later rule edit that would rename it does not reach the row. **`edition.kind` and `edition.language` are deliberately not on that list**, and spec C3 is what settled where they belong: `rule.set_kind`/`set_language` reached no row at all until `derive::write_edition_metadata`, so two of the accept form's five controls decided nothing — measured on real archives, an accepted `edition-of` proposal producing an edition whose `kind` was NULL beside the rule that said `official`. What bars a scan from the four columns above is having no way to tell a hand-set value from a derived one; this pair has one, since `librarydoc::apply` is the only other writer of a value into them and `migrate::absorbed(…, LIBRARY)` answers per work whether it has run — so they sit under that guard beside `work.series_id` and `work.volume` instead, which is what lets a rule edit reach them a second time. A kind outside the closed set is refused rather than stored: `librarydoc::of` refuses an unrecognised stored kind, so a work that can no longer be described is a worse outcome than a typo that decides nothing, and the refusal is counted rather than silent. `librarydoc.rs`'s series/credit/chapter editing (spec C3, the metadata-editing screen) has no CLI command or HTTP route that lets someone *set* it, which is O44 — *closed by spec C3 PR 2, 2026-08-28: the four `PATCH /api/library/*` routes are the callers, and `derive`'s read-back applies a document a rebuilt database has never seen.* It read: `taiyaku.library.json` is the one document designed for hand-editing and there is no route that applies a second one. **A scanned work's copy of that document lives at a second address**, one this crate's own `hand.rs` finds and writes:
`<root>/.taiyaku/<content_key>.library.json` — a real file this branch writes into a reader's library, beside their archives, not only into the database. `<stem>.library.json` beside a sidecar already answered for an imported work; a scanned work has no sidecar to sit beside, so `hand::path_for` addresses it off the hub edition's own root instead, and `hand::save` writes it and arms the `LIBRARY` marker in the same call — for a work with no address at all (an imported work, whose document is `export::work`'s to write) the marker still arms, only the file does not, which is `Saved::persisted` answering `false` with no failure. Migration 010 is what makes `work.title` and `edition.label` — the two columns C3 §5 puts a PATCH route over and that were previously always-populated, never-cleared — safe to hand-edit at all: each gets a `_hand`/`_derived` pair, `title_hand`/`title_derived` and `label_hand`/`label_derived`, because both underlying columns are `NOT NULL` and a hand edit's own withdrawal has to restore something rather than leave a `NOT NULL` column with nothing to fall back to. `migrate.rs` (the whole-branch review's C3 fix — a distinct, coincidentally-numbered thing from the roadmap spec above) is the one caller that reaches `apply`: on a work's first import, if `.progress.json`, `.notes.json`, `.truth.json` or `.library.json` sit beside its sidecar and the database holds no state of that document's own kind yet, each is read back once — rows are current, files are history, so a document the database already holds state for is left alone even when its file still exists. **Once, is a stored fact**: a `migrated_document` row per work per document, written the first time each is considered, so a reader who deletes their last note does not get it back at the next `serve` start, which is what testing emptiness instead did (review 2's C3). That row carries a second fact, `absorbed` — whether this library has ever had the file's *content*, read in here or written out by an export — because "this document is settled" and "the database has authority over the file at that path" are different claims, and `export --in-place` was reading the first as the second (review 3's C1, and schema version 2). A malformed file is reported and skipped rather than failing the import, and is the one outcome that records nothing, so fixing it and importing again still works — and now survives an export in between, which it did not. The import summary gained a word for the same reason: a settled document the database holds nothing for reports `unread` rather than `kept`, whose documented meaning is that the database already held it. Every progress, notes and truth call funnels through one connection behind one mutex, so WAL buys nothing and two different works no longer read in parallel (O42, unmeasured — the file store it replaced had independent I/O per work). **Between processes it buys plenty**, and that is the deployment this exists for: `serve` and `library import` default to the same file, so every connection carries a five-second busy timeout and opens its writes `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` — SQLite runs no busy handler for a deferred transaction promoting to a writer, so before this an import started while the server ran exited 1 on "database is locked" (review 2's I2). Each migration applies inside one transaction that ends by writing the version, so a migration that fails leaves the file exactly as it was rather than half-applied and unopenable (review 2's I1). **The first open of a fresh library is the one that races**, and both ways it could fail are now waited out rather than reported: the version is read a second time inside the migration's own transaction, so two processes that both saw an empty file do not both apply migration 1 (the second used to fail with `table series already exists` — the very message the module names as unrecoverable), and `journal_mode = WAL`, the one statement SQLite runs no busy handler for, is retried for the same five seconds rather than failing on the spot with `database is locked`. Measured before: 14 failures in 48 concurrent first opens, and 12 in 30 runs of the four-way test that now pins it; after: none in 40 runs of the same (review 3's I1) |
| `taiyaku-serve` | the HTTP API: works, sidecar, page by index, progress, notes (`<stem>.notes.json`, read and written whole under `If-Match`), a download — a whole edition as one `STORE` zip or one member's own bytes, both with an exact `Content-Length` known before the first byte and working `Range` (spec C2, all three routes: the two above and the OPDS-namespace mirror at `/opds/v1.2/works/{work}/{edition}/download`, which is the *same handler* registered a second time rather than a second implementation — it exists because a 401 on `/opds` carries `WWW-Authenticate` and a 401 on `/api` deliberately does not, so a client following an acquisition link into `/api` cold would never prompt. The acquisition link in `opds.rs::work_feed` points at it, with the `type` `download::advertised_type` says the route will actually send rather than a constant, since a single-member edition can be a PDF and a feed advertising it as a comic archive would be a claim the response's own header contradicts. **A reader whose `can_download` is withheld keeps the page link**: OPDS 1.2 requires an acquisition link on every entry — the reason this one pointed at a page in the first place — so it becomes the fallback rather than being deleted, while the web UI's own control is *absent* instead, a feed having a conformance floor a screen does not) — an OPDS 1.2 + PSE feed and generated covers, all behind a `PageSource` trait with **two** implementations — local disk, and a composite that resolves each member to disk or, inline within the same type, to Stump (see below). A caching split runs the length of the file: the four routes whose bytes are fixed by a member's `sha256` (the page, the tile, and OPDS's page and cover) are sent `private, no-cache` (`PAGE_CACHE_CONTROL`), with no freshness lifetime, so a client asks again before reusing one — the two page routes with an `ETag` as well, so that ask can be answered `304`, and the tile and OPDS's cover with none, since no validator is defined for either (`get_thumb`'s doc says what a tile's would have to name), so each ask is sent the whole image — save a library cover, page 0 at a cover size on the tile's route, which `serve_page` answers as it answers a page, with an `ETag`, and as `private, max-age=31536000, immutable` (`COVER_CACHE_CONTROL`) when its `?v=` names its bytes; a download is `private, no-cache`; and every route answering a document this server rewrites sets none, so `per_reader_by_default` sends it `private, no-store`, on the `304` as well as the `200`, which is the half that is easy to get wrong (O1). **Every route in `build_router` sits behind one guard since spec A2**, resolved from a session cookie or `Authorization: Basic` into a `Principal` — and `routes::guarded_routes` is the router's own source of truth so that `auth::tests::every_route_refuses_an_anonymous_request` walks the same list `build_router` folds, which is what makes a new unguarded route fail the suite on the commit that adds it rather than on a reviewer noticing. **Authentication had that enumeration from the start; the root grant did not, and six routes drifted from it before one existed** — four in `opds.rs` (`stream_page`, `cover`, `work_feed`, `works`), plus `routes::list_works`, plus a write route, `patch_alignments`, which returned a corrected sidecar in its response and wrote shared alignment rows for material the caller could not see. All six now refuse or filter, and `routes::grant_postures` classifies every guarded route as *Refuses*, *Filters*, *RefusesAndFilters* (among them `/api/works/{work}/progress`, `/notes` and `/truth`, each of which refuses a work outside the grant and, for a work the caller sees part of, leaves out what sits on an edition outside it) or *GrantIndependent* (with a stated reason, `/api/works/{work}/alignments` among them since O58 made the correction an administrator's, whom no grant limits); `auth::tests::every_route_declares_its_grant_posture` asserts that classification is set-equal to `guarded_routes`, so an unclassified route fails the build, and drives a real request from a restricted account for **every** *Refuses*, *Filters* and *RefusesAndFilters* entry, whichever way the table splits between the three (a route has moved between them before), a split and a total the test pins with assertions of its own so this sentence does not have to. Driven against both a whole work outside the grant and, since a whole-branch review found the first version of this table blind to the shape of its own headline defect, a work split across roots — rather than merely declaring them, with the rest (*GrantIndependent*) declared because there is no grant behaviour to drive — **all three figures were stale before C4 PR 2 corrected them**: they read 38/39/23/15 while the assertions in `auth::tests::every_route_declares_its_grant_posture` had moved to 19 driven and 26 declared over PR 1's seven new routes, which is the prose-outside-the-table drift the open-items ritual warns the sweep cannot predict; **and they were stale again when O60 closed**, reading 51 routes, 19 driven and one deliberate *KnownGap* against a table of 58 entries, 22 of them driven, with no such posture left, **so they are deleted here rather than corrected a third time**, not because driving them was skipped — the guard's own shape, closed for the boundary a checklist had only ever guessed at. `route_layer` rather than `layer`, so a path that does not exist still answers 404 instead of telling a caller every URL they invent names something real. The two 401 shapes differ deliberately: `/opds` carries `WWW-Authenticate`, which is what makes Panels prompt, and `/api` must not, because that header raises the browser's own dialog over a reader that cannot style, pre-fill or recover from it. Those five — six since O72, with `reopen` — resolve the row through `proposals::lookup`, which answers `Ok(None)` rather than an error for a row that is not there, so an unknown id is a real 404 instead of a 500 *(and since O72's fix round, `dismiss` and `reopen` also answer 404 for a row another process deleted after that check, through `curation::failed_unless_gone`)*. All six — seven since O72 — do their store work inside `spawn_blocking`, which is not decoration: measured with a canary task at 250,000 `scan_entry` rows, the dry run stalled the runtime 138.45 ms before and 0.02 ms after, and the handler's own duration did not move — so nothing but that instrument could have shown it. What the layer still cannot do is tell a refusal from a store fault, because the library hands it both as one `Err(String)`: a database failure during an accept reaches the client as a 409. That it runs the same `derive` a save runs is what makes "the preview is true" a property of the code rather than a promise two implementations have to keep. **Measured at a median of 281 ms** on 130 series and 1858 works (`docs/notes.md`), which is why C4 §6's "safe to call on every keystroke, debounced" ships as *previewed on demand* — safe, but not affordable. **PR B adds the seventh path, `PUT /api/library/rules`, and it is the first route in this product that applies a rule.** Every other rules route wrote the `rule` table and returned — `patch_rule`'s own doc said so in as many words — so editing a rule changed the rule table and nothing else until somebody scanned, while C4 §1's button promised "Save — apply to 71 works". The route is symmetric with the preview down to the body key, the `MAX_PROPOSED_RULES` bound and the `rule_from_json` reader, through one shared `read_proposed_rules(body, noun)` so the two cannot drift about what a proposed list is; `POST .../rules/import` stays what it is, a *document* import that mints fresh ids by design and so reopens every accepted proposal whose rule it replaces, which is correct for a foreign document and wrong for a save. **It is a method on a path that already existed**, so `guarded_routes` and the grant-posture table changed and `auth::tests`' `expected` array and its 19/32 counts did not — the list that can see a method arrive is `config_api::tests::every_config_api_route_refuses_a_reader`, which the spec's "a new route goes in four lists" never named. And `POST /api/library/roots/{id}/scan` is **the first time anything in the serving process has walked a filesystem tree**; it runs on a second connection so the shared one keeps serving, is single-flighted per root, and finally writes `root.last_scan_at` and `last_scan_status`, two columns that had existed since migration 1 with nothing in the tree reading or writing either. **PR 2 adds `users_api.rs` and `backup_api.rs`**, nine more admin-only paths and the end of C4's server half: user CRUD with C4 §4's three refusals, session and API-key revocation, and backup. The refusals live in the **store**, beside `account::promote`'s own, because the CLI is a second writer and a copy of an invariant in each is a copy that drifts — and they resolve into *two* rules rather than the spec's three: nothing may leave the library without an administrator who can log in (which covers both deleting the last one and demoting them, the same lockout by two routes), and an administrator cannot demote *themselves* even beside a second one, which needs to know who is asking and so takes an `acting_as` the CLI passes `None` for. `DELETE /api/library/users/{id}` states its counts first on the same `?dry_run=true` shape PR 1 chose for a root, and states five where a root states three — no work, edition or member is among them, which is the difference worth naming: deleting a person deletes none of the library. **PR C's screen found the one field this list never set**: `GET /api/library/users` passed `None` for the caller's session token, so every session it answered came back `current: false` — the flag C4 §6.2 wants precisely so an administrator can tell which row is the browser in front of them before revoking one. `session::list_sessions` had passed `token_of(&headers)` since spec A2 and this route had not; `assembled` takes it now, from `list_users` and `patch_user` alike, and only the caller's own account can hold a session whose sha256 matches, so passing it for every account is correct rather than merely harmless. Backup is `VACUUM INTO` through a new `taiyaku_library::backup`, a `taiyaku library backup` command and three routes, on a second connection so a file copy never holds the server's one mutex; **measured at a median of 6 ms** on the same 130-series library whose rule preview costs 281 ms (`docs/notes.md`), which is why the `POST` answers when the copy is done rather than streaming progress. `backup::prune` is the only file-deleting function in the store and deletes only names its own `list` returned. There is no restore route and no in-server schedule, both declined on purpose: restore is stop-move-start, and a cron entry runs the command. **All nine routes refuse a device credential as well as a non-admin**, through `session::refuse_a_device_credential` — the gate spec A2's second whole-branch review built for the self-service account routes, applied here because these are the same capability over *every* account and because the backup download is the password file. Measured before it was applied: `GET /api/library/users` under an administrator's API key answered 200 with every account's sessions, IP addresses and user-agents. **O93 closed the same gap on every other administrative route** — `config_api`'s twelve, `curation`'s six and `metadata`'s four — by collapsing three module-local copies of the role check into one `session::administering_or_forbidden` that asks both questions. A consequence worth knowing for anything that adds a route here: **the suite's default client is a browser**, and it was an API key until O93 — which is exactly why O93 survived four reviews, since every route test drove the credential these routes should have been refusing. `test_support::authenticating` opens a real session and sends its cookie with the `Host` and `Origin` a browser would; `key_authenticating` is what `opds/tests.rs` asks for by name, a key being the credential OPDS actually has. **`fingerprint` and `fingerprint_pass` are content matching's PR 2.** `fingerprint` is PR 1's page fingerprint — a file's border from a sample of its pages, the crop, the 16×16 dhash and a wide page's halves, and the `VERSION` of the records stored — moved here from `taiyaku-cli`, which calls it here. `fingerprint_pass` reads every page of each library with matching on (`library.match_by_content`, migration 28) in the background and stores one row per file through `taiyaku-library`'s `fingerprints`: four worker threads at `nice 19` and in the idle I/O class (`fingerprint_pass::priority`), each waiting before a file while the library job lock is held or a reader was served in the last 30 s, the whole shown in the scan feed as a job of its own kind that an admin can cancel. **`volume_match` and `match_pass` are content matching's PR 3.** `volume_match` is O340's volume scorer, copied from `taiyaku-cli`'s `match_experiment`, whose code the frozen bar was measured with, and held equal to it by a CLI test. `match_pass`, started when the fingerprint pass goes idle uncancelled, looks up each file not looked up yet, scores it against the files the lookup leads to and stores each pair from the floor of 0.6 up in `content_match` (migration 30), then derives where it stored a pair at the bar; the scan feed shows it as a job of its own kind that an admin can cancel. `curation`'s Split and Undo routes derive at once.
| `taiyaku-wasm` | the binding a browser reader loads: parse a sidecar, resolve a slot between editions, and say which path the answer walked |
| `taiyaku-cli` | the `taiyaku` binary: image decoding, fingerprinting an edition's pages on `rayon` threads through `taiyaku-serve`'s `fingerprint`, which holds the decode, crop and hash since content matching's PR 2, the content-addressed cache, the HTML report, argument parsing, and duplicate resolution — a copy's signature, the all-pairs judgement over one set, and the inventory walk that finds the sets |
| `web/` | the browser reader (React, Vite): single page, two-page spread, continuous-scroll and compare modes (compare: the page read beside the next edition's page for the same place, found as a swap would find it, the one read first in reading order, the two drawn and zoomed as a spread's two pages are), an arrow that steps by what is drawn rather than by slot, a swap that never writes position, a slot the edition being read has no page for filled from another edition and marked as borrowed (the gap state that used to stand there, offering the nearest paired slots either side as moves rather than jumps, is one press of that mark away), and a chrome of two bars shown and hidden together — a top bar of the way back, the work's title, the layout control and settings, and a bottom bar of filmstrip, progress line and five independently-switchable readouts (position, reading time, chapter, alignment health, note count) — behind the `Resolver` interface `taiyaku-wasm` implements. Every reading behaviour not yet in this list is one of ten `ReaderModule`s — of thirteen the registry holds — against a single declarative contract (`module.ts`): `direction` (a per-edition reading-direction override), `motion` (animate on/off, transition duration), `regroup` (parity breaks a reader inserts by hand), `readouts` (which of the five lines show), `prefetch` (depth ahead/behind plus a double-buffered, decode-before-swap image so a fast flick presents no blank frame), `annotations` (notes anchored to a slot of one edition and travelling to every other through the alignment, several to a page, each in a colour of the reader's choosing — a name in the file, never pixels — drawn as margin tabs plus an on-demand region tint — the tab in the letterbox beside the page, moving to the *outer* margin in two-page mode since closing the seam leaves a page no margin on its seam side — with five keys — write, reveal, review, and step back and forth through what has been written — and revealing off by default, since the margin tabs already say where the notes are without drawing on the page; notes save themselves a moment after the last change rather than on a button, so `history.ts`'s snapshots are what a reader abandons a change with; a region is swept out with a drag and pushed around with another, and while the editor is open every region on the page is visible and grabbable with one Save writing all of them, on an overlay that measures the artwork it sits over rather than the element around it — the same box, until `fit` made the element the whole cell and the two routinely different (§6 below); a note anchors to the whole slot, a point or an area, and its words are readable in a numbered list beside or below the page as well as in the region itself), `fit` (§6 below: how large a page is drawn inside its own box, and how far the two pages of a spread sit apart — `upscaleToFit` **on** by default, reversing the M5 design, so a 685×1024 scan fills a 1263px box instead of sitting at 1:1 in the middle of it, with `upscaleFilter` exposed beside it because that is a 23% enlargement of line art; and `gap` at `0`, where it is the two pages' *artwork* that meets rather than their elements — a distinction the design got wrong and a browser corrected), `layout` (which of the three reading modes is drawn — a module purely so that it *persists*, since it was component state and so was forgotten on every reload), `zoom` (§5 below: free continuous zoom and pan in single-page and two-page mode — wheel or pinch anchored at the pointer, a drag to pan with the note editor closed or a modifier held, and `=`, `-` and `0`; the view is one rect in *group* space, since a viewport can straddle both halves of a pair, and it is drawn as a single CSS transform on a wrapper, so `PageView`, `paintedBox` and every existing measurement are untouched — by zoom, which is what this claim was about; `fit` later changed both, §6; a page turn carries the rect and re-clamps, and a swap carries the visible content onto the other edition's page through the derived transform, or throws it away, a preference either way; continuous scroll keeps fit-whole, deliberately — its zoom is a different mechanism, since the strip's layout height is a function of scale and pan competes with scroll rather than sitting beside it), and `borrow` (the "Later" entry below is the record: where the viewed edition has no page for the slot, another edition's is drawn there and marked, and the mark is a button revealing the `Gap` view it replaced — hub-first order minus the viewed edition and minus the authority *(no fallback to the authority itself since 2026-08-13, marked here rather than rewritten: it used to lend when nothing else resolved, which it always could, and that was 228 of 276 corpus borrows — the page the reader had just left — so it was removed; the "Later" entry below is the record)*; on by default, so a gap now reaches a reader only through that mark on a work with a third edition, and directly otherwise, which is most of the corpus). The other three registry entries claim no reading behaviour. `settings` claims only the panel's own key. The remaining two are panels rather than page treatments. `credits` (§4 below): `C` lists the viewed edition's credit pages, a thumbnail and a page number each and no labels the sidecar cannot support, and `skip` keeps them out of the reading flow by being handed to `groups` rather than filtering its result — so the page area, the arrows and the filmstrip skip together — and since 2026-08-14 so do the offers out of a gap, which is O40 *(this said "not always" and named the exception: an arrow taken from a gap or a borrowed page reaches its destination through `nearestPaired` rather than `groups`/`stepToGroup`, so it could land on a credit page the reader asked to skip. `nearestPaired` is now handed the same skipped set `groups` is, from both of `App.tsx`'s call sites, so the key and the `Gap` screen's own offer buttons name one destination. It was unreachable on the corpus when it was found and still is, since `skip` defaults false and no corpus edition names credit pages; the fixture that reaches it lives in `App.test.tsx`)*, and two-page mode re-pairs around a skipped slot instead of stranding its neighbour. `help` (§6 below): `?` or `h` opens a list of every key the reader answers, generated from `keys.ts`'s one ordered table and from the registry rather than written out — so a binding that changes what it does cannot keep an old description, because there is one description — and listing only the modules that are switched on. `Settings.tsx` is generated from each module's `defaults` — a value's runtime type decides its control, never the module's id, a string a module declares `options` for becomes a select, and since O285 a number one declares in `sliders` becomes a slider — with a reset per section. **Spec C1's browse UI shell landed on top of it**, five files of it new and five more testing them: `Routes.tsx`'s `AppRoutes` resolves the four routes `react-router` now carries — `/` (the library grid), `/series/:id` and `/search`, both shipped by this branch (Tasks 1–10), and `/read/:work` (the reader, `key={work}` so `App.tsx` stays non-re-entrant across a swap between works); `Library.tsx` is the grid screen — a continue strip over `home`'s in-progress works, three chips (`all`/`multi`/`unread`) and an `added` sort that filter and sort client-side over data already held (§7's measured 127 series), all reading `library.ts`'s `/api/library/*` client; `EmptyState.tsx` renders the three first-run states spec C1 §8 asks for — no roots, roots but unscanned, and no matches — told apart by `/api/library/status` rather than by a grid response identical in the first two; and `Chrome.tsx` gains a `Library` button, docked opposite the reader's three existing panels and hidden mid-correction, so a reader has a way back out of the reader that is not only the `L` key. **This branch moved the sidebar out of `Library.tsx` and into `Shell.tsx`**, which now wraps all three library screens (not the reader) and owns the status fetch every one of them needs, so three screens share one fetch rather than risking three that disagree; `Sidebar.tsx` draws the list it is handed and no navigation path may require a root. `Series.tsx` is one series and its volumes — a grid or a table, `Cover.tsx` behind each and remembering a failed cover by its `src` rather than a flag so a retry survives a re-sort — an edition selector that dims a volume rather than removing it, and an optional `i` panel naming a verdict and a paired count from `/api/library/works/{slug}`. **Spec C2's download control lands in both layouts, and differently in each**: the grid gets one per tile for the edition the tile is already showing (`shown ?? w.editions[0]`, the expression its cover uses), because a tile shows one cover and the edition selector has already answered "which edition am I getting"; the table has no such edition — it renders one column *per* edition key — so there each cell's page count *becomes* the link, which adds no element to a layout built for comparing editions side by side. §8 of the download design asked for "the same control as a column" and that did not survive the table's shape. A plain `<a download>` in both, never a `fetch`: an anchor navigation carries the session cookie like every other browser request and the browser's own download manager takes the file, where a `fetch`-to-blob would buffer a 1.49 GB volume in the tab; the attribute is bare so the server's `Content-Disposition` name wins. Both are **absent** rather than disabled when `Me.can_download` is false — a disabled control invites a reader to find out why and nothing on this screen can tell them — and absent too when no gate sits above the screen, since `gate.ts`'s rule is that an unknown account is never read permissively. `Search.tsx` is `?q=` in the URL, debounced through `debounce.ts` at the reader's own 250 ms, a sequence number for out-of-order arrival and `run.cancel()` plus a bump on an emptied box so clearing mid-flight cannot land a stale answer over it; its hits draw through `SeriesGrid.tsx`, split out of `Library.tsx` this branch so the two screens sharing §5.4's `{ series, unfiled }` shape share one cover fallback rather than risking the `⇄` mark landing in two different places. *Search has since moved onto the Library view, by the sidebar and readability redesign (the "Later" entry below): `SearchBar.tsx` is the box, `searchHits.ts` holds the debounce and the sequence number, `Library.tsx` draws the hits through `SeriesGrid.tsx`, and `/search` redirects to `/` with its query and its library.* Both switches and the panel are preferences, not props: `browseModule.ts` is a second `module.ts` registry — `layout`, `editionSelector`, `panel`, `density`, `continueStrip`, `showRoots` — and `BrowseSettings.tsx` is generated from it exactly as `Settings.tsx` is generated from the reader's, `fieldsOf`/`fieldChanged`/`sliceReset` reused rather than reimplemented. *`showRoots` has since gone from the registry, `density` has become `coverSize`, a number the module declares a slider (O285), and since the sidebar and readability redesign `BrowseSettings.tsx` has gone too: a View button on the Library view and on a series page draws the preferences that act there, generated the same way (`ViewMenu.tsx`).* Migration 8 gives both FTS5 tables the `trigram` tokeniser — the schema is at version 9 — so a query of three characters or more finds any substring in either script, and `browse::search`'s `LIKE` path answers the two that trigram cannot, which is what `Search.tsx` types into without either being visible to the reader. Fifteen files new across the two (nine source, six tests), all under `web/src/`. **Spec C3's proposals inbox is the fourth library route**, `/proposals`, ten more files (four source, six tests): `Proposals.tsx` is the list — per-kind tabs each counting its own total regardless of which is selected, a score threshold defaulting to 1 on the `{0, 1, 2, 3}` scale with "Show weak proposals" dropping it to 0 rather than suppressing anything, and one row expanded at a time. `ProposalRow.tsx` draws the expanded row: two sides, subject and proposed target, each with a cover **and two interior pages** — the interiors being the point, since two editions' covers are two different illustrations and both in colour, and it is an interior that shows one edition to be the other colourised, confirmed against real archives at last (`notes.md`, 2026-08-26) after every screenshot until then had used placeholders — plus each side's directories, volume and page counts, format and root, the signed reasons behind the score, and a standing admission that nothing here compared the artwork. `AcceptForm.tsx` is the rule the accept would write: five controls (pattern, match-as, edition key, edition kind, language), a debounced dry run behind every edit, and an Accept disabled on any of the server's five refusal conditions *and* while the answer on screen measured a rule other than the one the button would send. `curation.ts` is the client for all of it. The screen asks only for `state: 'open'`, which is what an inbox is — but that leaves spec C3 §4's "a dismissal you disagree with later is a thing you have to be able to find" met at the store and API layers only, with no surface a person can reach, which is O72. *(O72 has since closed, on 2026-09-15: the inbox has an Open / Accepted / Dismissed control, and a dismissed row can be reopened — see its entry.)* The sidebar's `Proposals` entry **carries the open count**, which spec C3 §6 and the build design's file-structure table both asked for. *Since the sidebar and readability redesign the entry sits behind More, whose button carries the same count as a badge (`AccountMenu.tsx`).* *(It shipped without one for most of the branch, on the ground that `Sidebar.tsx` mounts around every screen and so a live count is a `listProposals` on every page load — a deviation recorded rather than silently taken, and reversed by the branch's whole-branch review. What settled it: that request is the flat one — `proposal`, joined to `series` for the two titles and grouped for the counts, with no rule compiled and no `scan_entry` walked, which is what the detail and dry-run routes both do — 0.10 ms at 8 rows and 0.23 ms at 25,008 against their 1.1–1.2 µs per entry, and it is admin-only, while the premise of §3's whole argument is that somebody learns the inbox is non-empty and nothing else in the app ever told them.)* The question the deviation left open was a real one and is answered rather than dropped: **what it counts** — the screen's header says *open*, but the list beneath it is narrowed to score 1 and above by default, so a badge counting every open proposal and a screen showing open-above-threshold disagree the moment a weak proposal exists, and the corpus raises those routinely, since a colour edition ingested to fewer volumes than its original scores exactly at the threshold. `curation.ts`'s `INBOX_MIN_SCORE` is one constant read by the badge's request and by the screen's own first request, so the badge is the number the header shows on arrival and pressing it can never land on an empty list. "Show weak proposals" moves the screen and not the badge, deliberately: that control is component state and starts false on every mount, so the list a person lands on is always the threshold's. `Shell.tsx` owns the fetch — one per shell mount, admin-only — and `shell.ts`'s `InboxRefreshContext` is how an accept or a dismiss moves it, since the two numbers are on screen together and a badge left stale beside a header that moved is a contradiction on one screen. **Spec C3 §6's ComicInfo confirmation is a section of `MetadataEditor.tsx`**, below Save and outside its `<form>` so pressing Save cannot trigger it, and absent rather than disabled for an account without `can_stamp`. **Everything in it renders from one derived phase** — `phaseOf` folds six state variables into eight named states (nothing asked, reading, read failed, empty plan, plan ready, rewrite in flight, rewrite refused, rewrite done) and every control, status line and paragraph reads that value. Three review passes had found defects there that were all one defect: each control stated its own condition over those six variables, each round's fix moved one condition, and the gates then disagreed — a plan read after a rewrite drew the archive list, the consequences and the irreversible warning with **no controls at all**, the two read controls could draw side by side under two alerts, and the one sentence saying a rewrite was running lived inside a button two reachable states did not render. Three separate comments arguing which combinations were reachable were each proven false by the pass after them, which is why the reachability claims that remain name a mechanism — a stamp supersedes any plan read it overtook the moment it is pressed, and a *successful* one also clears the plan it applied, so every plan on screen was read after the last rewrite that landed, while a refused one deliberately keeps the plan it refused, that being what a retry would send — rather than enumerating states. **Spec C4's settings area is the fifth library route**, `/config`, six more files (five source, six tests): `Config.tsx` is the area — one admin-only sidebar entry *(behind More since the sidebar and readability redesign)*, a sub-nav, and its own child routes declared from `config.ts`'s `TABS`, so a tab and the route behind it cannot drift apart and a bare `/config` redirects to whichever tab leads that list. No client-side admin guard, deliberately: `/proposals` has none either, and a non-admin who types the URL is shown the server's own 403 sentence rather than a bare status — a client that *decides* who may administer is the shape O93 was. Since the Configuration grouping's second PR its Libraries, Users and Backup screens are drawn on `settingsLayout.tsx`'s components: a page header with the page's title, description and actions and its way back where it has one, then sections, each a heading outside one box of rows with a label and its help beside the control, and last a removal box on a page that removes something. A removal's confirm draws its button and Cancel side by side, on two lines where they do not fit on one, and a library's or a directory's disclosure of what re-deriving would find after them. On a wide screen `SideBySide.tsx` draws an account's page or New account beside the Users table, and a directory's page beside its library's page; narrower, the page is drawn alone and the list is not mounted. Since its third PR the Rules tab is drawn on them too, at its own width rather than the pages' measure: the list and the rule being edited each in an untitled box, side by side where they fit, and the preview in a box titled Preview beneath them. Outside Configuration, `/account`, About and the licence page are drawn on them under a visible h1, each with h2 sections, and the reader's account panel, which draws `Account.tsx`'s controls, keeps its own look. A library's page and an account's are at their names (`configAddress.ts`), and New library and New account at `/config/new-library` and `/config/new-account`. `Libraries.tsx` is the tab where `Roots.tsx` was until F2a (`/config/roots` redirects to it), and since O219 it is four pages over one list: `LibraryTable.tsx`, a row per library that opens its page; `NewLibrary.tsx`, which makes a library from a name and one directory, typed or found with `DirPicker.tsx`'s browser of the directories the server may list; `LibraryPage.tsx`, a library's name, what it holds, a Scan library that walks each directory the library shows and derives once, Rename…, which edits the name in the title's place, a table of its directories with Add directory…, and Remove…; and `DirPage.tsx`, one directory's page, which is `RootRow.tsx`. A refused make or add is drawn as the server's sentence in the form that was submitted, and a refused rename in a callout laid over what is under the title, which moves nothing, and an answer whose page went before it came is said on the page the person is on;
