  before and 167.08 and 165.92 ms after, the after runs under the heavier
  load; the lines, the loads and what each run read are in `docs/notes.md`,
  "The first scan: the walk on NFS, the guard, and Cancel". The
  deployment's own figure waits for the owner's redo of the import. An
  entry whose local header is damaged is now listed and fails when read;
  the guard found none in the manga-test copy, so there was nothing for the
  owner to decide before the merge.
- **O311 — the reader's view said "Not read yet" during a first scan.
  Closed.** The view of an empty library a scan holds says Scanning, over
  the step line for an administrator and the step's word alone for anyone
  else, and waits for the feed's first answer since it was drawn, so it
  never says "Not read yet" or "Nothing here" first, unless the feed cannot
  be read, when it draws the status's state rather than wait for good. A
  search or a chip filter keeps its no-match state and says a scan is still
  running. When the scan ends the view reads again and the works appear,
  after the state between that O321 records. A first scan cancelled after
  its walk was saved reads "Not read yet" once it has stopped, since
  `scanned` now needs a last scan.
- **O312 — no page showed a scan's progress. Closed.** One scan feed,
  `GET /api/library/scans`, says which step each running job is in and the
  count the server keeps for it, files found, entries read, bytes hashed or
  works written, out of a total where one is known, and, while it lists or
  reads files, the directory it is on. An administrator is sent the counts,
  and anyone else each granted library's step. One poll per tab serves
  every page that draws it: the Libraries table, a library's page, a
  directory's page and the reader's empty view. It is faster while a job
  runs and stops while the tab is hidden, and a job's end, which its
  `ended` marker shows even for a job that began and ended between two
  polls, makes those pages read again. No figure on screen is one the
  server did not count: no bar, no percentage, no estimate.
- **O313 — nothing stopped a running scan. Closed.** Scan library, and each
  held directory's Scan directory, read Cancel while a job holds them. A
  cancel stops the whole job after the file it is on, or the listing it is
  in, keeps the digests and works it made, and pauses every directory of
  the job (O318 is the exception) until a press of Scan directory or Scan
  library, or a CLI `library scan`, covers it; the schedule stays as set,
  and the scheduler passes over a paused directory, its first tick after a
  start included. Each cancelled directory gets back the last scan it had
  before, its status word `cancelled` in the API, so a cancelled first scan
  still reads Never, and its pages say "Paused until Scan is pressed,
  since" and the time.
- **O257 — a directory's own scan, named beside a sibling's, holds Scan
  directory and Remove… with no "Scanning…". Closed.** A directory's page
  draws its own scan from the scan feed, whatever started or named it, so
  while a library scan walks it beside a sibling its Scan directory reads
  Cancel over the scan's step line. The test of it failed on `main`, where
  no step line was drawn at all.
- **O273 — an open page does not see a scan it did not start. Closed.**
  The library's and directory's pages, the Libraries table and the reader's
  empty view learn of each scan the server runs from the scan feed, whoever
  started it, and read Last scan, next scan and the reader's works again
  when it ends. `scanEnds.test.tsx`'s two O273 cases each failed on `main`
  on what the page drew after the scan. **What remains**: a page draws a
  `next_scan_at` that has passed as that time until it reads the directory
  again. A CLI `library scan`, which the feed does not show, and a stale
  page's Every choice saving over another tab's are O319.
- **O314 — series appear only once a job's hashing has ended. Open.** A
  first import shows no series until all of it is hashed. The second PR
  makes series appear as they finish, which needs the walk saved in
  batches; what to do with what a first scan has found so far is not yet
  decided. Not built.
- **O315 — "How it is read" says nothing of what its fields do. Open.**
  The third PR gives Edition key, Default kind and Default language help
  for someone setting up a library: what each does, what an empty key is
  read as, that two directories holding the same volumes need different
  keys, and that the key is best set before the first scan. Not built.
- **O316 — a long directory listing pushes the buttons down. Open.** On
  New library the browser's listing comes above Don’t scan yet and the
  form's buttons; the owner asked for the listing below the buttons, and
  the third PR is for it. Not built.
- **O317 — a more compact directory list, to be tried. Open.** The third
  PR tries one as a prototype on a live server, for the owner to judge.
  Not built.
- **O318 — a Cancel behind a long rules save loses its pause. Open.** A
  scan job waiting for the job lock behind a rules save, whose derive holds
  the store's write lock, and cancelled there, has its writes each wait
  out the 5 s busy timeout and fail, so its directories are not
  paused, and one it marked `waiting` reads that until its next scan or the
  server's next start. Found by the review of the job's cancel and parked:
  its fix would make a cancel wait for the holder. Not built.
- **O319 — a CLI scan, and a stale page's Every choice. Open.** Two parts
  of O273 the scan feed did not close. The feed lists only the server's
  own jobs, so a page open across a CLI `library scan` shows no scan and
  reads nothing again when it ends. A schedule saved in another tab ends no
  scan, so nothing reads a page open meanwhile again, and its Every choice
  saves the interval it keeps over the one saved since. Not built.
- **O320 — a derive of the whole store hashes a paused directory. Closed.**
  A paused directory is frozen until a pressed Scan or a CLI `library scan`
  covers it: every other derive reads it as its works last held it, through
  the reading the walk keeps when it clears a changed file's digest, and
  hashes none of it. So another library's Scan,
  the scheduled batch, a rules preview or save and a removal of another
  directory or library hash none of its files and read each held file by
  the reading its work was written from, save a folder volume's page count,
  which its member follows as before, and a rules save regroups its
  held files by those readings; another directory's file can still join
  one of its works. Any other file in it that would join a work waits for
  the Scan, hashed or not, unless its bytes are ones a work holds there
  (O336); a file gone from it is marked missing as before. A pressed Scan
  reads its directories fresh even where its unpause was refused. The row
  has the rest: the readings a pressed Scan drops and the ones it keeps,
  what a nested directory takes over, what an upgrade fills in and the one
  copy it cannot, and the report counts a paused directory can move.
  *Closed 2026-11-17 by the paused-directory freeze, whose paragraph
  follows O340's bullet, below.*
- **O321 — a state between the scan and what it left, as a job ends.
  Open.** For about one round trip after the feed stops showing a job, the
  reader's empty view goes from Scanning to "Not read yet" or "Nothing
  here" before its works, and a library's page whose job was cancelled
  shows no line before its paused line: the scan is taken off the page
  before the reads its end sent have landed. A library's page whose Scan
  library press had cleared a pause draws that pause's line again, a
  directory's page whose job was cancelled draws the job's `deriving` last
  scan and its next scan before Never, and the reader's view says "Nothing
  here" over "No series match this filter." with no filter set. The same
  shape as O259. Not built.
- **O322 — a reader's view loaded before its library was made never draws
  Scanning for it. Open.** The view asks the feed only of the libraries its
  status lists, so a page loaded before the library was made, or granted,
  never draws Scanning for it, though the feed lists the library: the drive
  saw "No library yet" until the job ended, which reads the status again. A
  fix would read the library list again when the feed names a library the
  page does not have. Not built.
- **O323 — "Cancelling…" waits for the feed, not the press. Closed, by
  design.** On the owner's ruling, a cancel is pending once the server has
  accepted it: the press holds the button and asks the feed as soon as the
  cancel's reply lands, so a page draws "Cancelling…" within one round trip
  of that, and a job that ends inside it is drawn as ended. No code
  changed.

O299's close opened O324.

- **O324 — a page of small text may carry more than the reader counts as
  reading. Open.** `MOST_READ_AT_ONCE`, 3,000 characters, tells a page
  turn from a drag of the scrollbar, and is a guess at a page's worth; a
  page at the smallest text on a tall screen may hold more, and its turn
  would then count as no reading.

Its review opened O325 and O326, both left for whoever picks up the books
work next to decide.

- **O325 — a short drag that selects text may be taken as a tap. Open.**
  The book reader takes a tap by `gestures.ts`' `TAP_SLOP`, 10 px on each
  axis, where it used 8 px as a straight line, so a diagonal mouse drag of
  up to 14 px is now a tap and what it selected is not offered for a note.
  Whether the book reader wants a figure of its own is undecided.
- **O326 — a straight quote that closes a quotation can count as one.
  Open.** `Anchors::of` takes an unpaired straight `"` as a quotation
  opened, so one closing a quotation an earlier block opened, or an inch
  mark, counts where a curly `”` would not. Telling an opening `"` from a
  closing one by the character before it would match the curly count, and
  waits on a run of `book_experiment` against the books corpus.

The whole-branch check of the books rich text opened O327 to O333.

- **O327 — a table, a list, a block quote or a poem is drawn as plain
  paragraphs. Open.** A book's rich text is marks over a block's text, so
  a table's cells, a list's items, a quote's indent and a poem's line
  breaks and indentation are not drawn as such. The design left them out
  on purpose.
- **O328 — an SVG image is not shown. Open.** An image is served by its
  index in the archive's image list, which holds the raster formats and
  not SVG, so a figure or an inline image whose `src` is an `.svg` is left
  out.
- **O329 — an image whose `src` differs from the archive's entry only by
  letter case is not shown. Open.** A `src` is matched to the archive's
  entries exactly, and `Baccano!` v22 and
  `Sword Art Online Alternative - Gun Gale Online` v14 name images in one
  case where the archive holds them in the other.
- **O330 — a scrolled book leaves its place, as images load, to the
  browser's scroll anchoring. Open.** Only a paged book is re-placed
  (`movesAnchor`); nothing here tests or records a scrolled one holding
  still as a figure above the reader gains its height.
- **O331 — an in-book link inside a footnote popup does nothing. Open.**
  The popup draws it as a link, but a tap on it does not jump.
- **O332 — every image of a book is fetched as it is drawn. Open.** None
  is fetched lazily, so a book of many illustrations asks for them as its
  text is drawn, on a phone included.
- **O333 — a figure not set in a link cannot be reached from the
  keyboard. Open.** It opens full size on a tap or a click, but takes no
  focus, so a reader with no pointer cannot open one. A figure set in a
  link is drawn inside the link, which takes focus.

The review of PR #253 opened O334 and O335, both recorded on the owner's
ruling of 2026-11-17.

- **O334 — requests for one book that miss the cache together each read
  it. Open.** `read` lets go of its cache's lock while it reads, so book
  or image requests for one book that arrive together after a restart, or
  once the cache has emptied past `KEPT` books, each read the book, split it
  into sentences and list its images. One read per file hash at a time
  would end it, provided a read that fails hands its error to the requests
  waiting on it; a cache of image names for the image route alone would
  split the numbering that route takes from `read`'s list. Not built.
- **O335 — the notes rule misreads three shapes of notes list. Open.**
  `in_note` reads a note set in a `div` or `section` that opens on a
  heading holding its back link as a group, so that link, where it is set
  as a reference, opens the text in a note card; a linked group whose
  first child is no heading (an `ol` or a `ul`, or one whose heading comes
  after a page-break `span`, an empty `<a id>` or an `img`) as a note, so
  a link to it opens a card instead of jumping; and an `li` grouping
  notes in nested lists as a note, its heading with it. The rule was
  rewritten twice in this PR's review and each rewrite regressed a case,
  so these are recorded rather than fixed. Not built.

Content matching's PR 1, a measurement, opened O338, O339 and O340.

- **O338 — editions are matched only by name. Open.** Copies of one
  volume are joined end to end, a chapter directory with no volume makes
  no work, and two series join only on an exact title. The
  content-matching design matches by page content instead, over five PRs;
  its PR 1 found no rule that lets a content match go automatic (O340).
  *Narrowed on 2026-11-17, and left open: PR 2 stores a fingerprint of
  every page of each library with matching on, in a background pass.*
  *Narrowed on 2026-11-19, and left open: PR 3 joins volumes whose pages
  match at or above the bar automatically, with Split and Undo.*
- **O339 — an omnibus is never linked to the volumes it covers. Open.**
  The design's ruling 5 keeps an omnibus whole, in its own series, and an
  `alignment` row sits inside one work. A follow-up to the
  content-matching PRs.
- **O340 — the volume-against-volume rule passed, and the owner's ruling
  on pack cuts is what remains. Open.** PR 1's volume rule failed on
  held-out on two pairs of Bisque Doll fan extras the owner judged
  different. On the owner's ruling of 2026-11-17, a short measurement
  then tested a rule limited to volume-against-volume pairs, its bar
  frozen on the series already scored and tested on series this
  measurement had not scored when the bar was frozen. The rule passed:
  no wrong pair of 12,186 reached the frozen bar of 0.87, so PR 3 may
  apply volume matches at or above the bar automatically. Of the 59 true
  pairs, 52 cleared the bar and 7 did not, two of those at V 0 with the
  verdict Refused (`notes.md`, "Edition matching by content: the
  volume-against-volume test (2026-11-18)", "The result"). Whether pack
  cuts go automatic on the pack rule's frozen bar is the owner's to
  decide, before PR 4.
  *Narrowed on 2026-11-19, and left open.*
  *Narrowed on 2026-11-19, and left open: PR 3 applies volume matches at
  or above the bar automatically, with Split; the ruling on pack cuts
  remains.*

**The paused-directory freeze of 2026-11-17**
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-16-paused-directory-frozen-design.md`,
the owner's option (a) for O320, built as "paused means frozen") closed
O270 first, which the freeze would otherwise have turned into a deleted
member, and then O320; both bullets are above, O270's under lane 2's
Finish fix wave and O320's under the first scan's progress and Cancel. It
opened O336, from its plan's pre-flight scan, and O341, from its
whole-branch review; their bullets follow.

- **O336 — a new file whose bytes a paused directory already holds joins
  their work before the Scan. Open.** A file added to a paused directory and
  hashed before the cancel, byte for byte a file a work holds under that
  directory, passes the freeze and joins the work, where every other new
  file that would join a work waits for the Scan. It is a visible addition,
  with nothing lost, and was accepted when found. Not built.
- **O341 — a `library scan` walk beside a server derive can leave a file
  with no reading. Open.** The CLI walks before it takes the derive lease,
  so its walk can commit between two works of a server derive of the same
  directory. A file the walk finds changed after the derive read it has its
  digest cleared and that reading held, and the derive, writing its work,
  drops the held reading by path: the row keeps no reading while its work
  holds one. The CLI's own derive hashes it again; where that derive does
  not run and a Cancel pauses the directory first, the freeze finds nothing
  to read the file by, and its work is rewritten without it. Found by
  reading the code. Not built.

**The Korean dictionary of 2026-11-17**
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-17-korean-dictionary-design.md`) opened
O376, O377 and O378 from its measurement on Harry Potter 1, and the owner's
ruling of that day closed O377; their bullets follow. `docs/notes.md`,
"Korean dictionary: installed and measured on Harry Potter 1", has the
measurement.

- **O376 — a conjugated Korean verb or adjective can miss. Open.**
  `lookup_korean` takes off particles and nothing else, so a verb is found
  only in the forms kaikki lists: 있다 has 85 rows and 37 distinct forms, and
  the median over the 3,443 verbs with forms is 98 rows and 79 distinct
  forms. 있는데 is listed and 있었는데 is not, and 없다고, 싶지, 자랑스럽게 and
  기이하거나, which carry no tense, are in no `form` row either. Taking endings
  off needs a table that respects irregular stems, which is not designed.
  Not built.
- **O377 — a transliterated name is in no dictionary. Closed, on the owner's
  ruling.** A missing name answers 200 with an empty list and the panel says
  "Not in the dictionary." A name that collides with a noun shows the noun:
  해리 is only "nautical mile", and 론's five entries hold the name Ron
  fourth, after three senses the book does not mean. Among the words
  particle-stripping newly finds across Harry Potter 1, 해리 is 1,465 and
  론 454. The owner ruled out a per-book name list.
- **O378 — a Korean numeral with a counter or a particle. Open.** The digit
  stays in the key, so the word misses unless the dictionary has the number
  and counter as one word (7월, and 11월이 through 11월). A tap in a Korean
  book takes in the digits joined to the word and sends what is printed: 10년
  sends 10년 and answers "Not in the dictionary", from the digit or the letter,
  with the whole run lit. A tap on a bare number such as 2000 is no look-up. A
  drag across the digit misses the same way. A drag over the letters alone
  sends only those letters, so 년 dragged out of 10년 is looked up as 년.
  Looking a counter up without its number is not built.

**The resize polish of 2026-11-16**
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-16-resize-polish-design.md`) opened and
closed O303 to O306, for what the owner found trying its prototype, and
opened O307 to O309 and O337, the last two from the owner's hand-check on
an iPhone; their bullets follow. `docs/notes.md`, "O303 to O308", has the
height the phone layout turns at and why, the Firefox figures, the defect
each test was watched failing against, and what a phone's turn does.

- **O303 — the Continue row's fade came and went at once. Closed.** Each
  side of the row fades in and out over 200 ms, and flips at once under
  reduced motion. A card's focus ring lifts the fade at once, and only the
  fade's return eases. In the phone layout the fade is half as wide.
- **O304 — covers jumped to their new columns. Closed.** At a window
  resize or a Cover size step that changes a list's columns, each cover on
  or near the screen glides from where it is drawn to its new place, and
  the Continue row moves with them on the same clock and curve. A change
  in the number of covers that changes a list's height, either edge of
  the phone layout, reduced motion and a phone's turn snap. The page
  holds still: nothing scrolls sideways, and a scrolled page rests where
  the same resize without the glide leaves it. The owner kept the turn's
  snap in the hand-check. Two trades are put to the owner with the PR:
  at rest the browser now holds a tile's top, not the caption at the
  view's top, so where a cover's height changes the page rests by that
  change from where main leaves it; and in the phone layout the Continue
  row is laid at once wherever its covers lie above the view, so the row
  slides in fewer places than the spec first recommended.
- **O305 — a phone held sideways got the desktop layout. Closed.** Below
  900 px wide or below 500 px tall a window gets the phone layout, so a
  phone in landscape gets the phone bar, the drawer, filled covers and the
  document scroller, and a turn no longer swaps the scroller. That ends
  the gap at the foot after a turn, but not the trip to the top: iOS
  Safari also sets the page's scroll itself at a turn, and O306's keeper
  puts the place back. Every stylesheet site and script reads one
  condition, and a test holds them together. An Android tablet with a
  600 dp short side, held sideways, falls under 500 px too in Chrome and
  gets the phone layout, which is put to the owner with the PR.
- **O306 — a swap of the scroller sent the view to the top. Closed.** A
  window crossing into or out of the phone layout keeps the element at the
  top of the view at the top, over ten crossings, and Back after a swap
  lands there. Since 2026-11-17, on the owner's ruling to fix it in this
  PR, a phone's turn keeps the place too, where iOS Safari had moved the
  page itself, and a turn and its return land where the reader started,
  so turning back and forth does not drift. On the owner's iPhone the
  home turned from its middle, the home with a sliver of the Continue row
  in view, and a Cover size change after a turn all passed. The phone did
  not show a turn's return keeping the place a Cover size step left, since
  every turn around the step was at the page's top; a browser test holds
  it.
- **O307 — the open drawer is wider than the sidebar. Closed.** The drawer
  was `min(20rem, 85vw)` wide, against the sidebar column's `14rem`, and
  O305 brought it to a phone held sideways. Since the drawer polish it is
  the column's 14rem plus the left safe area it pads inside itself. What
  remains is unmeasured: the left inset on a phone held sideways.
- **O308 — a kept scroll restored into another layout. Open.** Back, or
  leaving the reader, after the layout changed elsewhere lands at a pixel
  offset that shows other covers, as on main for any resize. Keeping the
  place by an element instead is a PR's worth of work.
- **O309 — the drawer's foot on a phone held sideways. Closed.** On the
  owner's iPhone in landscape, about 440 px tall, the drawer's foot (the
  build's label, More and the theme switch) took most of the drawer's
  height, so the library was hard to browse from it. Since the drawer
  polish, under 500 px tall the foot follows the navigation and scrolls
  into view at the end of the list, and More's panel there opens whole or
  scrolls inside itself. On 2026-11-18 the owner checked the final build
  on the iPhone against a list that included More opened at the end of
  the drawer held sideways, and said "ok it seems good across these".
- **O337 — the phone bar on an iOS turn. Closed.** On the owner's iPhone
  the phone bar disappeared as the phone turned and popped back after. A
  logger on a hand-check rig found the bar at the window's top, 52 px tall
  and sticky, in every record it took through each turn, the turn's resize
  included, so it did not move in layout. Every pinned position the owner
  tried popped, which the drawer-polish spec reads as iOS drawing a layer
  pinned to the viewport again after a turn. Since the drawer polish the
  bar moves with the scroll inside a track and, once the page is still
  with any of it in view, rests as part of the page, so that a turn draws
  it with the page; a turn keeps the share of it in view. On the prototype
  the owner found "a very slight pop now but it's better". On 2026-11-18
  the owner checked the final build on the iPhone against a list that
  included turns with the bar in view and out of it, and said "ok it seems
  good across these", with no mention of a slight pop this time.

**The drawer polish of 2026-11-17**
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-17-drawer-polish-design.md`) closed O307,
O309 and O337, which the resize polish opened; their bullets are above,
with that PR's. The owner chose each part by trying a prototype on the
iPhone, and the PR built the chosen parts again under tests; the owner
then checked the final build on the iPhone. `docs/notes.md`, "O307, O309
and O337", has the options the owner tried and why each was chosen, the
rig's figures, the order of a turn on the phone, the owner's check of the
final build, and the defect each test was watched failing against.

**Content matching's PR 2, fingerprints in the server**
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-17-content-matching-fingerprints-design.md`),
stores a fingerprint of every page of each library with matching on, in a
background pass, and matches nothing. It narrowed O338, whose bullet is
above, and opened O342 from its plan, O343 from a task's review, O344 from
a task's build, O345 and O346 from the whole-branch review, O347 from the
review of its fixes and O348 from its gate; their bullets follow.

- **O342 — a long download stops holding the fingerprint pass back after
  30 s. Open.** A download marks a reader as its handler starts, and its
  body is sent after that, so once 30 s have passed since the mark the
  pass starts new files beside it. Found while planning. Not built.
- **O343 — a Move, a link, a rules save and a CLI scan make files due
  without starting a pass. Open.** Their files wait for the next scan the
  server runs to its end, or its next start: a pass starts only when a
  scan job ends without a Cancel, at startup and when a library's switch
  is turned on. Found by a task review, checked by reading the code. Not
  built.
- **O344 — a folder volume is hashed with every page in memory. Open.**
  `member_digest` reads a folder's pages whole before it hashes them; the
  pass holds one such folder at a time, under the large-page lock, but
  nothing bounds its size. Found while building the pass. Not built.
- **O345 — the pass's writes commit from a lowered thread. Open.** Each
  row and digest the pass writes is committed by a thread at the idle I/O
  class, which holds the store's write lock through the commit. Whether a
  commit stalls behind other I/O is to be measured on the deployment host
  while a reader reads; if it does, the writes move to a thread at normal
  priority. Found by the whole-branch review. Not built.
- **O346 — a large page's bytes are read outside the large-page lock.
  Open.** Only the decode runs alone, so each of the pass's workers can
  hold an archival page's encoded bytes at once; it matters only with
  archival pages on the NAS. Found by the whole-branch review. Not built.
- **O347 — a folder that cannot be read whole is read on every pass.
  Open.** A file whose listing fails, or whose walk ends on a read error,
  is stored unreadable or partial for the build; a folder in the same state
  fails its digest check, so nothing is stored, it stays due, and each pass
  reads it again and says the error on stderr. Found by the review of this
  PR's fixes. Not built.
- **O348 — a browser test of the covers' glide fails run alone. Open.**
  `reseat.browser.test.tsx`'s "starts where drawn after a scroll while the
  covers glide, then the next change" fails when it runs alone and passes
  with the rest of its file, so it leans on a test before it; under load
  it has also failed in a whole run of the browser project. It came with
  #259 and is to be fixed in a PR of its own. Found by this PR's gate. Not
  built.

**RAR through libarchive, PR 1, of 2026-11-17**
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-17-rar-libarchive-design.md`) lets
`taiyaku-read` read RAR in a build with its `rar-libarchive` feature, the
container image among them, while a library's scan still makes no member
of one *(since RAR PR 2, O391, it does in such a build)*; such a build
does import and serve a sidecar that names a RAR
member, as its own `align --write` can write, since neither
`library import` nor the server checks a member's format. Every read holds
an entry's data to the CRC32 its header declares, because libarchive does
not compare a stored entry's data with it. The PR opened O380 from the
design, O381 and O382 from the compress-tools spike and the owner's rulings
on it, O351 from its task reviews, and O383 to O386 from its second
whole-branch review and the checksum check that review led to; their
bullets follow. `docs/notes.md`, "RAR through libarchive: the
compress-tools spike (2026-11-17)", has the spike's results and the fork's
fixes, and "RAR through libarchive: the checksum check (2026-11-18)" what
the owner's RARs hold and how they read through it.

- **O380 — a solid RAR5 decodes every entry before the page it reads.
  Open.** Nothing keeps what a read decoded, so each page read from a solid
  RAR5 decodes again every entry before it. None of the owner's 21 RARs is
  solid, so the design reads a solid one rather than refusing it, and
  accepts the cost until one appears in a library. A solid RAR4 is not read:
  libarchive refuses it at its second entry, so taiyaku refuses it whole.
  The follow-up the design names: unpack a solid RAR5 once, on first open.
  Not built. *`member_page` has listed first since RAR PR 1, and listing a
  solid RAR5 decodes every entry (measured on libarchive 3.8.11), so serving
  any page of one has always decoded it whole; RAR PR 2 adds a library that
  counts and serves one.*
- **O381 — a RAR entry taiyaku could not read was listed as a page. Closed
  by RAR PR 2.** taiyaku's own walk of the block headers runs at listing as
  well as at reads, so an archive holding an encrypted entry is refused at
  the count on any libarchive version; an empty file reads as empty without
  asking libarchive; and a file reference or hard link reads the bytes of
  the earlier entry of that name it names, while one with no such target, or
  of another size than its target, is refused at the count. The owner's fork
  was not changed: libarchive gives no target for a `rar -oi` file
  reference.
- **O382 — compress-tools comes from the owner's fork. Open.** The release
  crashes on a RAR4 name outside ASCII under the C locale, registers no skip
  callback and can leave a thread using a freed locale; the fork, pinned by
  commit, fixes them. While it stands, cargo-deny reports no RustSec
  advisory against `compress-tools`, since it matches a crates.io advisory
  to crates.io packages only. It closes when a release carries the fixes and
  the `[patch.crates-io]` entry goes.
- **O351 — two RAR4 gaps. Open.** A RAR4 cut exactly between two blocks
  lists, counts and reads as a shorter archive with no error, since a RAR4
  need not end with an end block. One cut less than seven bytes into a
  block's header lists and counts short too, but every read of it is
  refused, because the walk of the block headers behind the checksum check
  cannot finish. A RAR5 is refused when its end-of-archive block is missing
  or followed by anything but zero bytes. The owner ruled the RAR4 check of
  the listing out for now. And a RAR4 entry name in a legacy code page
  refuses the whole archive unless its bytes happen to be valid UTF-8, when
  the page reads under a wrong name; a zip keeps such a page under a garbled
  name. Every name in the owner's ten RAR4 comics is ASCII. Not built.
  *Narrowed on 2026-11-19 by RAR PR 2, and left open: the listing now walks
  the block headers, so a RAR4 cut where the walk cannot finish is refused
  at the count; one cut exactly between two blocks still lists short.*
- **O383 — a RAR5 entry that declares only BLAKE2 is not checked. Open.** The
  check compares CRC32s, and a RAR5 made with `rar -htb` declares a BLAKE2sp
  hash instead, so a damaged stored page of such an archive reads as good.
  All 3,063 files in the owner's 21 RARs carry a CRC32 and none a BLAKE2
  hash. Checking one needs a new dependency or hand-written hashing. Not
  built.
- **O384 — a RAR replaced during `member_page` could return the wrong page.
  Closed by RAR PR 2.** `member_page` lists a RAR and reads the page by its
  position in that listing through one open of the file, as a zip is read,
  so a file renamed over the path between the two cannot answer for it.
- **O385 — two RAR5 entries of one name gave answers that disagreed. Closed
  by RAR PR 2.** Two readable entries of one name refuse the archive at its
  count, by a rule in `pages.rs` that every listing of a RAR passes through,
  as the owner ruled.
- **O386 — no libarchive release decodes RAR 2.0 compression. Open.** Every
  page of Fantastic Four v1 360, a RAR4 comic whose entries use it, fails
  with `Prefix found` on 3.6.2, 3.7.4 and 3.8.11, though `unrar t` passes
  it. On the owner's word it was converted to a stored zip on 2026-11-19,
  the original kept; a user's RAR 2.0 archive is still refused. One page
  each of Zelda v01 and v03 failed on bookworm's 3.6.2; the image and CI
  moved to Debian trixie, whose 3.7.4 reads every page of both (`notes.md`,
  "libarchive 3.7.4: the image and CI move to Debian trixie (2026-11-19)").
  A libarchive release that decodes RAR 2.0 would settle it. Not built.
  *Narrowed on 2026-11-19, and left open.* *Narrowed again by RAR PR 2:
  such an archive is refused at the count, from the unpack version and
  method its file headers declare, with nothing decoded, and the scan writes
  the cause to stderr.*

**RAR through libarchive, PR 2, of 2026-11-19**
(`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-19-rar-libarchive-pr2.md`, on the owner's
rulings P2-R1 to P2-R6) lets a library read RAR in a build with the
`rar-libarchive` feature. It opened and closed O391, closed O295, O381, O384
and O385, and narrowed O351 and O386, whose bullets above say so, and O131,
whose row does; O391's bullet follows. `docs/notes.md`, "RAR PR 2: libraries
read RAR (2026-11-19)", has the rulings, the decisions as built and the checks
on the owner's RARs.

- **O391 — RAR reading in libraries. Closed.** In a build with the feature,
  the image among them, a scan counts a RAR, the derive makes members of it,
  the fingerprint pass reads it, and the server serves and downloads its
  pages, as for a zip. A RAR of a kind libarchive could not read whole is
  refused at the count, and the scan writes the file and the cause to
  stderr. The reader signature gains a RAR part naming the libarchive
  version `pkg-config` gave the build, so a store scanned by a build without
  the feature counts its RARs at the next scan by a build with it. In every
  build, a download passed through takes its type and extension from the
  format the scan stored, where the file is as that scan saw it, and
  otherwise from a sniff of the file, not from its name, which closes O295;
  and a scan writes to stderr why the reader refused to count a zip, or a
  RAR in a build with the feature.

**JPEG XL pages of 2026-11-17**
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-17-jxl-pages-design.md`, on the owner's
choice to read formats as they are rather than convert them) closed O130,
narrowed O56, and opened O390, from its plan, O349, from its run over a real
archive, O350, from its whole-branch review, and O388, from the review of
its fix round; their bullets follow.

- **O130 — taiyaku read no JPEG XL page. Closed.** An archive or folder of
  `.jxl` pages is counted and read like any other, and every place that
  decodes a page decodes JPEG XL, through jxl-oxide. A client whose `Accept`
  names `image/jxl` is sent such a page as stored where it is not resized;
  any other is sent a JPEG made from it once and cached. Covers are never
  JPEG XL, downloads keep the stored pages, and every JPEG the server makes
  from a page with transparency lays it on white. Every zip is counted once
  more at the first scan after the upgrade, with nothing hashed again, so an
  archive of JPEG XL pages main left uncounted becomes a member; a folder
  holding both JPEG and JPEG XL pages is hashed once at that scan. jxl-oxide
  was chosen over `jxl` by a comparison over the Bisque Doll original's
  pages: both decode them within a level of `djxl`, and only jxl-oxide counts
  its own working memory against the limit. The row and `docs/notes.md`,
  "JPEG XL pages: the decoder, the clients and a real archive (2026-11-17)",
  have the rest.
- **O390 — a zip holding JPEG and JPEG XL pages keeps renderings named for
  its old pages. Open.** When such a zip's `.jxl` pages start counting, its
  pages renumber, which the design accepts, and its cached renderings and
  page tags, keyed by its digest and the page's offset, go on naming the
  pages they were made from until the file changes. A folder holding both
  is hashed once at the first scan after the upgrade, so its renderings and
  tags get new keys. A saved place keeps its slot in both. The design found
  no such entry in the owner's library. Accepted, with no code; a library
  that holds such a zip would reopen it.
- **O349 — memory taken by JPEG XL decodes is kept after they end. Closed.**
  The `taiyaku` binary allocates through jemalloc, whose background threads
  give memory freed after a burst back to the system on a timer, even where
  no request follows. Measured again on the desktop: 30 s after the last
  response the branch's server held 51,806 kB against main's 784,452 kB, each
  the mean of two runs (`notes.md`, "jemalloc as the allocator: memory after
  a burst (2026-11-19)"). What remains: the NAS is not measured; at a
  settled load the burst took 1.070 times as long under jemalloc, 18.075 s
  against main's 16.89 s, each the mean of two runs; C code, the bundled
  SQLite and the image's libarchive among it, still allocates through
  glibc's malloc, since jemalloc's symbols are prefixed; and a cap on decodes
  stays deferred until a peak on the NAS shows a need.
- **O350 — jxl-oxide reads an embedded ICC profile outside every limit.
  Closed.** Since the colour profile cap PR, a page whose header declares an
  encoded profile above 64 KiB is refused before jxl-oxide reads it, in the
  image hook and in `jxl::rebuilt_jpeg`, which between them stand before
  every place taiyaku hands jxl-oxide a page, and a page with a real Display
  P3 profile still decodes. Within the cap jxl-oxide still decodes the
  profile and parses it outside every limit; the owner's ruling of
  2026-11-19 lowered the cap from 1 MiB to 64 KiB so that the worst profile
  it passes, decoded and parsed once, stays under the boxes' 16 MiB, and a
  page through the hook was not measured. jxl-oxide also still parses a
  header again after every 4 KiB of input until it is whole, bounded by the
  cap and not measured. A hand-built page measured the fill the item had
  only read in the source; the row and `docs/notes.md`, "JPEG XL pages: a
  cap on the embedded colour profile (O350, 2026-11-19)", have the rest.
- **O388 — a zip replaced at the same size and mtime with another page
  count is read again by every pass. Open.** Replaced before its first
  fingerprint read, the file keeps the count no scan took again, while the
  row the pass stores numbers the pages it now holds, so the two never
  agree. Each pass pays one file's read. An intact copy of the old bytes
  shares its digest and so its row: read from the replaced file, the row
  misnumbers the copy; read from the copy, it misnumbers the replaced file,
  and neither is read again. No fix has been chosen.

**The gates of the O349 and O350 branches** went red on two of book
search's tests, which neither branch touches; with the owner's agreement
of 2026-11-19 the defect is filed as O413, and its bullet follows.

- **O413 — book search's wall-clock bounds fail when the machine is loaded.
  Open.** Neither branch changes anything under `web/`. The O349 branch's
  gate failed at 547.3 ms against the 300 ms bound, at a load of about 31
  (`T1-gate-run1.log`), and at 101.95 ms against the 100 ms bound, with
  the load at about 14 just after the gate ended (`gate-after-rebase-2.log`),
  both in `.superpowers/sdd/mimalloc-evidence/`. The O350 branch's failed at
  115.4 ms against 100 and 381.9 ms against 300 in one run, at a load of
  about 30 (`gate-fixwave.log`), and at 387.6 ms against 300, with the load
  at 38.55 as the gate was run again (`gate-after-rebase.log`), both in
  `.superpowers/sdd/jxl-icc-cap-evidence/`. The loads are the ones the
  branches' ledgers record; none of these files is committed. Each time the
  same tree passed when the gate ran again. Gate logs of three other
  branches from 2026-11-18 hold failures of the same bounds, in
  `.superpowers/sdd/content-matching-o340-evidence/logs/`,
  `jxl-pages-evidence/rebase-2026-11-18/fix-round/` and
  `rar-pr2-evidence/bump/`. No fix has been chosen; the options include a
  looser bound, a check that counts the work a search does rather than
  timing it, as the file's "folds a block once, however many searches read
  it" test counts `normalize` calls, and timing the search outside the
  gate.

**Content matching's PR 3, volume joins**
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-19-content-matching-volume-joins-design.md`),
joins the editions of a volume whose pages match at or above the bar
automatically, and an admin can Split a join and Undo the Split. It narrowed
O338 and O340, whose bullets are above, and opened O392 to O407 and O414:
O392 and O393 from its plan, O394 and O401 to O404 from its tasks' reviews,
O395 from its prototype, O396 from its run on real material, O399 from its
mutation sweep, O397, O398, O400, O405 and O406 from its final review, O407
from the owner's ruling that Undo takes back a whole Split, and O414 from
a mutation sweep; their bullets follow.

- **O392 — a pair the lookup never offers stays unjoined. Open.** A file is
  looked up once and scored against its three leaders by votes, so a true
  pair neither lookup offers is never scored. Kobayashi v03, v05 and v11
  stayed apart on the test library with no pair stored, though the store
  cannot say whether the lookup offered them.
- **O393 — a Split lives only in the store. Open.** As a proposal's
  dismissal does: a library rebuilt from its files and documents joins the
  pair again where it applies.
- **O394 — a solver alignment outlives a pair that stops applying with
  nothing moved. Open.** Where names hold both files in one work and
  matching is switched off, or a re-downloaded file never scores at the
  bar, the row stays, and derive cannot tell its own rows from those
  `align --write` stores.
- **O395 — a raw of double-page images is aligned in fragments. Open.**
  Stored runs are whole pages, cut at every split spread, so Tongari v09's
  raw at V 0.967 shows ⇄ with 4 of 172 pages paired.
- **O396 — the fingerprint pass hashes a volume a second time. Closed.** A
  worker given a file listed with no digest now reads the digest its entry
  holds before it hashes, so a volume a derive hashed while the pass waited
  is not hashed again. A derive that starts while a worker is hashing can
  still take that one file's digest first, and two identical files listed
  with no digest that two workers take at once are both read.
- **O397 — the match pass decodes every print before it asks whether a file
  is due, and nothing tests its libraries' wiring. Open.** A pass with
  nothing to look up has still read and decoded every taking-part file's
  prints. No test holds that the pass gives each lookup its file's
  libraries; a pair across libraries never joins, and were that wiring to
  break, a file of another library could take one of a true partner's three
  places among the leaders, so that pair would never be scored.
- **O398 — pairs stored at the bar wait for another derive where the pass
  stops before its own. Open.** A restart, or a Cancel while that derive
  waits for the job lock or the lease, leaves them unjoined until another
  derive, such as a scan's, a Split's or an Undo's.
- **O399 — `scripts/mutants.sh` fails its unmutated baseline at thirty-two
  test threads. Open.** Three `tests::serve_*` tests fail at niceness 19
  with thirty-two threads in one process, on `main`'s tree as on this
  branch's.
- **O400 — the derive's content-match counts reach an admin in part. Open.**
  The CLI's derive line has no clause for joins, followers or alignments
  not written; the scan report's "Alignments not written for volumes joined
  by content" counts pairs that names put together too, a label that waits
  for the owner's words; and nothing reports the stamp aliases an edition's
  move carries.
- **O401 — a digest two members hold is looked up with the first member's
  libraries. Open.** Derive applies none of its pairs where both are files
  a scan holds, so those lookups are spent on pairs that never apply, and a
  library reaching only the second member never offers it.
- **O402 — two choices content joins make without a ruling. Open.** A join's
  host ranks editions by the kind the rules resolve, not an admin's hand
  kind, which an alignment's direction does read; and a volume in two
  directories follows whichever is its primary. Each wants the owner's
  ruling.
- **O403 — what stands is met again by every derive. Open.** A work that does
  not project fails every derive while it holds a pair to align, a scan's
  included, and a move refused once takes the write lock and rolls back at
  every derive.
- **O404 — a hand value on an edition a join moves is lost. Open.**
  `fold::move_edition` carries the readers' positions, notes, truth and
  stamp aliases onto the edition's new work, but not an admin's label, kind
  or language.
- **O405 — a content-match line can name a pair wrongly. Open.** A Split
  takes in a pair that names hold in one work, which derive cannot keep
  apart, so the panel lists the work as kept apart from itself; and a file
  split from its host and keyed anew leaves its edition on the host
  still marked, offering Split on a pair already split.
- **O406 — the Series panel after a derive, a Split or an Undo. Open.** An
  open page keeps each volume's panel detail from before a scan's or the
  match pass's derive; after a Split or an Undo the panel says nothing of a
  move the derive refused.
- **O407 — Splits among many editions need a page of their own. Open.** Undo
  takes back a whole Split with one derive, and a volume's panel draws one
  line per Split, so a Split among many editions, or many Splits on one
  volume, makes long lines, and nothing takes back part of a Split. The
  owner plans a better manager for larger splits later.
- **O414 — `scripts/mutants.sh` reported a sweep that tested nothing as
  clean. Closed by its own PR.** One run of PR 3's sweep of its fix for a
  volume arriving where a work was placed by hand failed its unmutated
  baseline and tested no mutant, yet ended "no survivor outside the
  baseline" with exit 0, because the script read cargo-mutants' exit status
  only where `missed.txt` was absent. It now reads that status, refuses an
  earlier run's output, and reads `outcomes.json`: a failed baseline exits
  4, and a run whose every mutant fails to build, or that made no output and
  does not say why, exits 2, while a run whose scope holds no mutant, in
  cargo-mutants' own words, says so and exits 0. A run that stopped partway
  yet exited 0, 2 or 3 would still be read as a verdict.

**The CI build volumes' runs on the forge**
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-20-ci-volumes-design.md`) timed the four
Rust jobs on both runners from kept build volumes, and from empty ones where
one of the runs found them empty, and opened O415; its bullet follows.

- **O415 — the job bound's 134 s no longer held. Closed by the owner's
  ruling.** `timeout-minutes: 10` was 4.5 times a worst job of 134 s, at
  `ci.yml`'s head and in `docs/ci.md`'s "Bounding a test's runtime". On the
  NAS runner the `test` job took 8 min 25 s with its build volume empty and
  6 min 44 s with it kept (runs 1026 and 1028). The owner ruled on 2026-11-20
  that 10 minutes is fine, so the bound stays, and both places now give that
  ruling as its reason.

## What comes next

Roughly in order. All four are now settled — one closed by a measurement that
came out against shipping it, one shipped as two commands, the third the large
piece, shipped across four milestones, and the fourth shipped as an eighth
command plus a field in the format — and they stay here rather than being
deleted, for the reason the open-items table gives: a list that only ever grows
says nothing about whether anything lands. **All four are now shipped whole**:
the fourth's reader half — the panel and a `skip` that governs something —
landed on 2026-08-07 with O25, which had blocked it, closed the same day.

**A fifth arrived from below rather than from this list.** L1 geometry sat under
"Later" from 2026-07-30, the day this file was written, until it shipped on
2026-08-08; it is §5. The entry that advertised it is kept and corrected at the
foot of "Later" rather than deleted, because both halves of what it promised
turned out to be wrong and that is worth reading. Everything still genuinely
unbuilt is under "Later".

**A sixth was never on any list, here or under "Later".** It is three reader
complaints raised after L1 shipped — pages not filling the page, a gap down the
middle of a spread, and no way to find out what the keys do — grouped onto one
branch because each is small and none touches the alignment. It is §6. That it
came from reading the corpus rather than from a review is the pattern `notes.md`
keeps recording: the browser is where the reader's own defects surface, and no
amount of unit testing substitutes.

### 1. Refuse on margins, not just counts — measured, and margin does not fit

The candidate fix was measured against the corpus rather than shipped. Margins
are quantised to whole 256ths, and the corpus's one confirmed needle (Color
Walk, margin 0.004) sits exactly one bit below its weakest confirmed-good
pairing (Monster's 2:1 repagination, margin 0.008). No safety factor fits in a
one-bit gap, so no margin threshold ships. Average run length carries the case
instead — every confirmed-good pairing at 36.0 to 200.0 slots, everything else
at 6.8 or below — and on this corpus runs per hundred pages separates as well,
once refusals are gated on coverage; the swap was made because run length is
stated in slots rather than per hundred pages, not because the old measure
could not tell these rows apart. `verdict()` already called the needle case
`Fragmented`; both `align` paths now print that verdict, so the case that
opened this item is no longer silent.
**Closed.** Twenty-two needles have since been measured, and they settle it
harder than the survey could: a needle outscores four confirmed-good pairings
on margin and seven on separation, so neither calibration statistic can be made
to refuse this case. Only run structure separates, by a factor of twenty. What
remains open is narrower and belongs to the reader rather than the solver —
`Fragmented` is reported and nothing refuses on it, so a reader consuming a
sidecar has to look at the verdict rather than assume acceptance means
correspondence.

### 2. Duplicate resolution as a command — shipped, and one word in the protocol was wrong

The protocol was worked out by hand across 109 volumes and is now two commands.
`inventory` finds the sets in a release directory; `duplicates` resolves one set
into a decision. On the One Piece collection the hand run took 19 duplicate sets
down to 13 real choices, with 2 mislabelled files flagged rather than silently
ranked, and the commands run the same three steps:

1. **Signature** — file count, total bytes, sorted size list, confirmed by a
   content hash over page bytes wherever it matches. Settles exact duplicates
   without decoding a page, and a copy it settles is never fingerprinted at all.
2. **All-pairs alignment within the set** — not everything against the first
   copy, which hides clusters. Spreads always split, with no flag to turn that
   off, because the headline case in this collection is 200 images against 101.
3. **Cluster on identity, flag what is not this volume, and rank the rest** by
   content first — slots, then pairings against an `--against` reference — and
   only then by how cleanly it aligns. What is not this volume is whatever
   refused against every other copy; with a reference edition it is whatever
   pairs nothing with the reference, which is the only thing that can answer a
   two-copy set where each refuses the other.

**Say what shipped, not what the design sketched.** `notes.md` used *identity*
two ways, and the command uses only the stricter one. `align` reports unmatched
slots for the **A side alone**, so a pair that covers all of A prints as
"nothing unmatched" whether or not B carries slots of its own that nothing
reaches; read that way, containment looks like identity. The command asks both
sides and reports five relations — identity, `within`, `contains`, distinct,
refused. Of the five pairs in the corpus that come within two slots of covering
each other, **three are containment and two are identity**: One Piece v092 is
200 slots wholly within 202, Bocchi's two real scans are 124 within 125, and
Chainsaw Man's `src-a` is 198 within `src-b`'s 199, while Chainsaw Man's two
198-slot scans and One Piece v077's c1 and c2 do cover each other on both sides.
`notes.md` called four of the five identity. Clustering merges on identity
alone, because a container holds content the other copy lacks and collapsing the
two would discard the very difference the choice is about — the ranking already
prefers the container, on slot count.

**Six gated corpus checks measure this, and all six pass.** v077 resolves to
clusters `{0}` and `{1, 2}`, the identity pair at 1 run and 234 of 234 against
104 and 100 fragmented runs for either copy against c0. v092 comes out
containment, two clusters, c1 first on 202 slots. Bocchi's *Gaiden* file refuses
against both real scans, is flagged, and is excluded from the ranking. A sixth
runs those same three Bocchi copies a second time, against the *Gaiden* file's
own English edition, and measures the flagging inverting — the two real scans
flagged and the *Gaiden* file the only one ranked, at 185 slots against the 125
it ranked behind with no reference. Four Chainsaw Man raws against the English
release rank `src-b` first on 199 slots, with `src-a` and `src-c` collapsed into
one identity cluster. `inventory` over `op-duplicates` finds 34 candidates
across 16 volumes, every one of them duplicated. The full figures are in
`notes.md`, "Duplicate resolution as a command, and half the identity claims
above are containment".

**What it does not do, stated with the example rather than as an abstraction.**
The ranking prefers whichever copy holds more material, including material that
may not belong: on v077 the command names copy 0 the best, on 236 slots against
234 — and copy 0 is the different-crop outlier that fragments against both of
the others. The pairs table above the ranking shows that plainly and `--against`
a reference edition settles it, but a ranking read on its own picks the outlier
here. `inventory` has the matching caveat: it groups on the deepest directory
that holds a whole edition, which is not always the copy directory a person
would name, and `--pattern` matches against that directory's name rather than
the copy's.

### 3. The reader — shipped

A PWA consuming the sidecar, with the correction UI as part of it rather than
after it. This was the multi-week piece and the point of everything above, and
every stage it was split into — M5a, M5b, M5c, M5d — has now landed.

**Its blocker is cleared.** Until 2026-07-30 there was no way to produce a
sidecar with three editions and no way to resolve through one, so on any work
with more than two editions — which the primary development corpus is, at five —
the reader could not have answered "show me this page in edition C". `align
--write` now merges and `resolve` now composes.

**The swap UX is settled, not open — this line previously said `notes.md` left
it undecided, which had stopped being true.** `Space` toggles between the
current edition and the last one and `1`..`9` jump directly, settled on
2026-07-30 and reopened and re-settled on 2026-08-01: the case against a
hold-to-open picker was "it costs the one-key promise," which only holds on a
device with a key, so a later brainstorm's picker did not lose the argument, it
answered a different device. Desktop-first was confirmed the same day, which is
what keeps the toggle for this reader; the picker moves rather than dying,
reassigned to a future native iOS reader where a sheet is the right gesture for
a device with no key to promise. See
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-30-reader-design.md`, "Swap is a toggle key
plus number keys."

**M1, M2 and M3 have landed.** M1 moved page reading into `taiyaku-read`, so the
aligner and anything serving pages derive the normative sequence from one place,
and added addressing a single page by index — serving page 47 of a 195-page
volume costs one page rather than the volume. M2 added `taiyaku-serve` and the
`serve` command: the work list, the sidecar verbatim, a page by index with its
content type, and a reading position stored beside the sidecar, all behind a
`PageSource` trait so running beside Stump and replacing it are the same code
above that line. A gated corpus check compares every page the server serves
against the page the aligner sequenced — 617 of them on Go-Toubun v01, no
disagreement.

M3 added Stump support and an OPDS 1.2 + PSE feed. **Say what shipped, not what
the design sketched:** the design named a third `PageSource` implementation,
`StumpLibrary`, alongside `LocalLibrary` and a composite. It was never built,
because it could not have answered anything on its own — resolving a member to
a Stump book needs the resolution map, which only the composite holds, so a
standalone Stump-only source would have been unusable by construction. What
shipped is `CompositeSource`, which resolves each member to whichever source
holds it, with the Stump-backed branch (GraphQL to resolve, REST to fetch
bytes) living inline inside it. `PageSource` has **two** implementations, not
three.

**What would make the third one worth building**, recorded so the decision can
be revisited on evidence rather than re-argued: a work whose members live only
in Stump and never locally. That is not reachable today for a reason deeper
than the trait — `resolve_member` needs the member's *local* file, for its size
and for the page-hash confirmation that makes a match trustworthy, so a member
taiyaku does not hold can never resolve at all. M3 therefore offloads page
reads for files you already have; it does not let taiyaku serve a work it does
not have. Serving one would need a different way to match a member to a book,
which is its own design question and wants its own pass — at which point a
standalone Stump source stops being nomenclature and starts being load-bearing. **Say what the feed actually earns, not what the milestone originally
claimed:** M3's stated end state was "Panels reads the library", but that was
already true without taiyaku — this Stump instance serves OPDS-PSE itself, and
a third-party reader could point at it today. What taiyaku's feed adds is
grouping several editions under one work, which neither Stump nor Komga can
express: on this instance `Go-Toubun no Hanayome` and its Full Color Edition
are two unrelated 14-book series, with no link between them and no way to make
one inside either server. The gated `PageSource` equivalence check measured
this for real against the live instance: 187 pages of `en-mono` agree
byte-for-byte between `LocalLibrary` and the composite's Stump-backed path,
and 8 members — the raw and all seven fan chapters — are absent from Stump and
correctly recorded absent rather than retried per page. See `notes.md` for the
coverage table and what the instance exposes.

**M4 has landed, and it is the smallest of them.** `Route::resolve_slot` makes
the slot rather than the page the thing a reader resolves, which matters exactly
where a run ends mid-spread: in the primary sidecar, `en-mono`'s page 4 is a
joined spread whose right half pairs with raw 5 and whose left half pairs with
nothing, so a reader resolving the page instead of the half would show one and
call it the other. `taiyaku-wasm` puts that in the browser's reach without
`taiyaku-core` taking a `wasm-bindgen` dependency, and the gate now builds both
for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` — the binding for a second reason, since a
signature that cannot cross the JS boundary compiles natively and fails only
there. What was **not** claimed at the time: nothing had executed the module
under a wasm runtime. The agreement check compares the binding against the
core on every slot of every ordered pair of a two-edition fixture, which
catches conversion drift and not codegen.
**M5a closed that gap by running it.** `scripts/smoke-wasm.mjs` loads the
compiled `.wasm`, parses the fixture and checks six properties against it —
`editions`, both slot counts, a half-aware `slotAt`, `indexOf` and one
`resolveSlot` — against the same values `binding.rs` already pins natively.
All six passed, and the generated `.d.ts` matched what the plan had assumed
about the binding's shape. See `notes.md`, "M5a, measured directly: the
reader's own evidence, not the scratch ledger's". **What is still not
claimed:** CI does not run this script — `docs/ci.md` records why — so a
codegen break would still go green there; the discipline stays a local one,
run after any change to `lib.rs`.

**The Panels measurement has started, and found a defect before it found a
number.** Panels read from this server over the LAN on 2026-07-31 — see
`notes.md`, "Panels, measured: the feed was one-based and should not have been".

The first session's finding was not a performance figure but a correctness bug:
**OPDS-PSE counts pages from 0 and taiyaku's feed counted from 1**, so Panels
met a 404 on opening every book, and every page it then displayed was the one
before the page it believed it was on. Thirty per cent of the session's requests
were that 404. Fixed, and the test that used to assert the wrong convention now
asserts the right one at both ends of the range.

**The targets are now measured**, over a deliberate fast-flick session of 177
page requests. The server is not the constraint by a wide margin: median
processing 1.43 ms against a tightest client request rate of 40 ms. Panels
issues no concurrent page requests — zero overlaps, and the arrival floor holds
at 40 ms even flicking as fast as the UI allows — and never asks for a reduced
size, so it takes whatever resolution the server holds, 247 KB a page here.

One thing is deliberately **not** claimed: whether Panels *blocks* on each
response. At 1.43 ms no request was ever still open when the next arrived, so a
blocking client and a UI-paced one are indistinguishable in this log. Measuring
it would need a deliberately slowed response, which is not worth building.

**M5a has landed.** The swap works: `Space` toggles between the current
edition and the last one, `1`..`9` jump directly, and a swap never writes
position — round-tripping through any number of editions is lossless by
construction, not by care. All three reading modes ship — single page,
two-page spread (right-page-first under `rtl`), continuous scroll — with a
joined spread drawn once, not as two halves, in every one of them. Landing on
a slot with no counterpart in the edition just swapped to reports a gap rather
than silently moving to the nearest slot, and offers the nearest paired slot
either side as a move the reader takes deliberately rather than one that
happens to it. A floating chrome shell — a filmstrip and a slot readout,
brought in and taken away together by `Tab` — never reflows the page
underneath it, and its tiles are served by a per-page thumbnail route measured
against the real corpus (O11, below). Reading position is restored on load
from the server and written back on `navigate` — debounced, so arrowing
through a run of pages is one `PUT`, not one per keypress — and never on
`swap`, which has nothing to record.

**What M5a leaves open.** There is no prefetch and no double buffer: a fast
flick between adjacent pages can still show a blank or half-decoded frame
before the next one paints, closed in M5b behind two `<img>` elements and
`img.decode()`. Continuous-scroll mode does not write reading position back
either: entering the mode scrolls to where you were, but hand-scrolling never
updates the stored slot, so a reader who reads by scrolling and closes the tab
loses their place — an `IntersectionObserver` is the fix, and it belongs to a
later milestone, same as prefetch.

**What M5b's decode gate leaves open, in two-page mode.** The gate is per
`PageView` instance, not per pair: an ordinary spread's two halves each run
`presentWhenDecoded` independently, so a turn can present one freshly-decoded
half beside one still-showing old half for as long as the slower of the two
takes to decode. That is not the defect the gate exists to close — neither
half is ever blank or half-painted on its own, which is the guarantee
`decode.ts` actually makes — but simultaneity across a pair is not something
this build guarantees, and no comment here should be read as claiming it is.
Left independent deliberately rather than gated together: gating would make
the faster half wait on the slower one on every ordinary turn, a real latency
cost paid on every pair for a mismatch nothing has measured a reader
noticing, particularly now that `App.tsx`'s separate swap and prefetch decode
queues (`swapQueue`/`prefetchQueue`) keep either half's decode from being
starved by prefetch traffic in the first place. A measurement showing the
mismatch is large enough to matter is the reason to revisit this, not a
guess made ahead of one — see `App.tsx`'s `renderGroup` for the same
reasoning kept beside the code it describes.

**The filmstrip's tiles do not reopen O9 — this paragraph previously said
they could, and that was wrong.** Each tile resolves its own thumbnail, which
on a cold strip is a burst of up to N requests for N *distinct* pages —
structurally the same shape as the cover burst O9 already measured and
declined to guard: one request per member, nothing to coalesce. O9's own
reopening condition is concurrent requests **for one key**, which this is not.
Nothing on this branch reopens O9; it stays open on the reasoning already
recorded there. The mitigation this paragraph also claimed for the burst
turned out weaker than stated, though **not as weak as this paragraph said
until O140 re-measured it**. It read "does not defer thumbnail requests at
all in the environment tested", which is true of the rail M5a measured and
false of a long one: at 390×844 on a **237-tile** rail, 101 of 237 thumbnails
were requested and the tiles past index 101 stayed 4 px wide and issued
nothing until scrolled to (`notes.md`, "O140: the chrome's build cost").
So `loading="lazy"` does bound a cold-strip burst, at about a hundred
requests rather than at the rail's length — **neither figure should be cited
again without saying which rail length and viewport it was taken at**. See
also `notes.md`, "M5a, measured directly: the reader's own evidence, not the
scratch ledger's".

**O14, not O9, is the item M5a actually gave a trigger to, and from a caller
nobody had named.** `web/src/nearest.ts`'s `nearestPaired` calls `display`
once per candidate slot either side of a gap, and each cross-edition `display`
is one `Binding::resolve` — up to `slotCount` route rebuilds, unmemoised, on
every render of the gap state. See O14's entry above.

**M5b has landed.** Every reading behaviour M5a shipped as fixed code is now
a `ReaderModule` against one declarative contract (`module.ts`): a `defaults`
object, an optional set of claimed keys, checked for a keybinding collision
or a duplicate id at import time rather than at runtime. Five modules exist
against it — `direction` (a per-edition reading-direction override, `d`,
layered over `work.reading` and never written back to it), `motion`
(animation on/off and transition duration, an empty style object rather than
an inline `transition: none` so a reader's own `prefers-reduced-motion` still
governs when animation is off), `regroup` (parity breaks a reader inserts by
hand, `b`, for the one case a joined spread cannot derive), `readouts` (the
four lines above, each independently switchable, with an unknown alignment
verdict reported as `verdict unknown` rather than silence that could be
mistaken for `sound`), and `prefetch` (a tunable window ahead and behind the
current slot, decoded off-screen through `decode.ts`'s double-buffered
`<img>` pair and swapped in only once `img.decode()` resolves — the fast
flick M5a left flickering). `Sidecar::chapter_at` in `taiyaku-core`, carried
across the `wasm-bindgen` boundary and into `Resolver`, feeds the chapter
readout; it names a member, not a chapter number, and the one chapter-
organised edition in the primary corpus (`en-fan`, reached from the hub by a
`fragmented` alignment) is marked `~` in the readout rather than shown as
settled fact, for the reason the twenty-two needles already established.
`routes.rs` now sends an `ETag` on every page response, keyed on a member's
`sha256` and its offset within that member, which is what let O1 be measured
rather than argued (below). `Binding` memoises its last-resolved route,
closing O14 (above).

**Task 11 closes the milestone: the settings panel, generated rather than
hand-written per module, and every module verified switching off on real
material.** `Settings.tsx` renders one section per registered module with a
control inferred from each `defaults` key's runtime type — boolean → check-
box, number → numeric input, string → text (a select is what the design
calls for once a module declares one with options; none does yet, and the
contract carries no field to declare options against, so that path is not
built ahead of a case that exists only in the design) — never branching on
which module or key it is looking at. A sixth registry entry, `settings`,
claims one key (`s`) for the panel itself the same way any module claims a
key, its own `defaults` empty, so the generated panel renders no section for
it. Two of the five modules hold a preference keyed per edition
(`direction`'s `override`, `regroup`'s `breaks`) rather than a flat value;
the panel has no way to know "edition" is what a given `Record` is keyed by
without being told per module, so these render a read-only entry count and
are cleared by the section's own Reset rather than edited field by field —
the module's own key (`d`, `b`) still edits one entry at a time, as before
this task. All five modules were then driven in a real browser against
`corpus/gotoubun-v01`: each one's behaviour stopped when switched off, took
effect when tuned, and survived a reload, with no remnant left on screen
when off. `prefetch`'s `maxConcurrent` needed the decode queues themselves
to change from a value fixed at mount to one rebuilt when the setting
changes — without that, tuning it in the panel would have been a control
that did nothing until the next reload, the exact kind of generated-but-
broken input this milestone was built to avoid. See `notes.md`, "M5b Task
11: the settings panel, generated, and all five modules measured switching
off", for the module-by-module table.

**A whole-branch review before this branch merged found "generated rather
than hand-written per module" true only of `Settings.tsx`, and fixed the gap
rather than merely narrowing the sentence.** `App.tsx`'s own preference
state — a `useState`/`loadPrefs` pair, a `savePrefs` effect, and a case in
each of `handleSettingChange`'s and `handleSettingReset`'s switches, per
module — was still hand-written as of the paragraph above, so a seventh
module (`fit`, `filters`, both still deferred) would have gotten a
normal-looking control in the generated panel that changed nothing until
someone also hand-wired those four places: the same "generated but broken"
failure already fixed once, above, for `prefetch.maxConcurrent`, moved one
layer up into code only a manual browser pass could catch. Fixed by making
that state one map built from `registry.all()`, keyed by module id
(`module.ts`'s `sliceFor`), and by moving the registry itself out of
`App.tsx` into `modules/registry.ts`, so registering a module no longer
touches `App.tsx` at all. Proved with a throwaway seventh module registered
only in `modules/registry.ts`: it appeared in the generated panel and its
preference persisted across a reload with zero lines changed in `App.tsx`,
then was removed. `modules/prefetch.ts`'s doc comment, which still described
toggling `enabled` by hand-editing storage — true before Task 11's panel
shipped, false since — was corrected too. All five real modules were
re-driven in a real browser after the refactor and still switch off, tune
live, and persist, matching the table above.

**What M5b did not reach.** The filmstrip's tile burst is still exactly
where M5a left it: `prefetch`'s decode cap governs `PageView`'s page
decodes through `swapQueue`/`prefetchQueue`, and `Filmstrip.tsx` never
receives either — it renders thumbnails as plain `<img loading="lazy">`, so
a cold strip still fires one request per distinct tile, and the
`loading="lazy"` finding above still stands, unaddressed, confirmed again
rather than assumed carried over. Continuous-scroll mode **still** does not
write reading position back — entering the mode restores where you were,
but hand-scrolling never updates the stored slot, unchanged from M5a and
needing the same `IntersectionObserver` that milestone already named. The
`fit` and `filters` modules the design specifies are not built; the contract
they would slot into is what M5b spent five modules proving out instead.

**M5d has landed.** A reader can now point at the right counterpart in the
filmstrip and have the fix written into `taiyaku.json` as `by: "hand"`,
surviving a re-solve and a second device writing at the same time. The
arithmetic is one pure function in `taiyaku-core` (`correct_runs`) and one
document operation built on it (`Sidecar::correct`), so no second
implementation of run-splitting exists to disagree with `compose`. The
browser sends the *assertion* — slot `a` of `from` pairs with slot `b` of
`to` — never a computed run list, so the split is applied once, server-side,
against the authoritative document: a deliberate departure from the design's
"the client computes a run split, `PATCH` to serve", made because a
client-computed list would put the 1:1 eviction rule in a second
implementation a future reader could get wrong, and would leave `If-Match` as
the only thing standing between a stale client and a wholesale replacement of
the edge. `taiyaku-serve` gained its first mutating route, `PATCH
/api/works/{work}/alignments`, guarded by `If-Match` against an `ETag` on the
sidecar, which forced the in-memory document to become replaceable
(`RwLock<Arc<Sidecar>>`) rather than loaded once at startup; `GET
/api/works/{work}` now carries an `ETag` too. O13 closes in the same branch
(above), because the correction UI is what first constructs a `Source::Hand`.
**Driving the UI against the real corpus found one defect the whole review
chain had missed.** A correction silently stripped every `margin` on the edge
it touched — `entries_from_runs` writes `margin: None` for every entry it
builds, having no confidence figure to hand them, and the correction sent the
whole edge through it. One correction took `raw-mono -> en-fan` from 8
margins to 0 while the untouched `raw-mono -> en-mono` kept all 3. Fixed: a
margin now carries forward only where both spans are identical, and the two
runs a correction actually reshapes lose theirs honestly rather than keeping
a stale figure. See `notes.md` for the full measurement. **The same pass
found that two hand corrections are enough to take a sound alignment to
`fragmented`**, opened as O23 above rather than answered on a guess.

**A defect that manual pass reported was not M5d's, and shipped on its own
commit after it: an arrow moved by slot where a group is what is drawn.** A
joined spread is two slots and one wide image, so stepping by slot redrew what
was already on screen and the press appeared to do nothing — *"I have to right
arrow twice to go by it"* — and in `two` mode a press advanced the pair by one,
redrawing half of it. `stepToGroup` (`web/src/pairing.ts`, pure, ten tests)
steps by group instead, measured on `en-mono`, which has spreads at pages 45,
46 and 49: pressing right from displayed slot 45 walks `45 → 46 → 47 → 49 →
51`, one image per press, symmetric backwards. **Landing on the group's first
slot fixes a second thing the report did not name** — both halves of a joined
spread draw the same image but `resolve_slot` answers them *differently*, so a
reader who could not see which half they stood on got one of two different
answers on a swap from a screen that looked identical either way. **What it
costs:** the second half of a joined spread is no longer reachable by arrow,
nor is its own swap answer; it stays addressable where addressing it is the
point — the correction filmstrip puts one tile per slot, and `two` mode draws
the halves in separate cells. Confirmed acceptable during the same manual
pass. *That cost is unchanged by O28, which closed the clamp this same commit
introduced — see its entry above; what changed is only what an arrow does where
there is no next group to land in.* The grouping reaches `applyIntent` as an optional parameter with the
slot arithmetic kept as the fallback, because how the page is grouped right
now — mode, direction override, hand-inserted parity breaks — is something
nothing below the component tree knows.

**M5c has landed, and with it the thing the sidecar was for.** A note written
on `raw-mono` is readable while reading `en-mono` or `en-fan` — resolved
through the same `Resolver.resolve` the swap makes, so no second
implementation of travel exists to disagree with the first. Notes live in
`<stem>.notes.json` beside the sidecar, the placement `progress` established,
written whole under `If-Match` through the atomic writer O2 introduced; the
`GET` synthesises an empty document where no file exists, so a client's *first*
write is an ordinary conditional write rather than a second precondition
spelling. A note is anchored to a **slot**, never a page, while its region —
when it has one — is fractions of the **page that slot is drawn on**, so a
re-scan or a different served resolution cannot move a marker. *That last figure
read "fractions of that slot" until 2026-08-08; the code has measured against
the drawn page since M5c, and the two differ only on a joined spread, whose two
slots share one wide image. `notes.ts`'s `Region` carries the correction and
what it costs L1.*

**What it deliberately does not do, stated rather than discovered.** A
region does **not** travel, so a travelled note draws a margin tab and never a
tint, because drawing the untransformed box would put it over the wrong panel.
*Until 2026-08-08 the reason given here was that transforming one between
